Maria Del Rio se confie à Soir mag : « On est revenu à l’essence même de ‘L’amour est dans le pré’ » Maria Del Rio rempile pour une troisième saison à l’animation de « L’amour est dans le pré ». - RTL-TVI Dès ce 20 septembre, « L’amour est dans le pré » revient pour une 18 e saison. La troisième présentée par Maria Del Rio, l’animatrice emblématique du « Good Morning » sur Radio Contact. Une édition lors de laquelle elle a à nouveau été frappée par de belles histoires d’amour naissantes et par des parcours de vie atypiques. Après toutes ces saisons de « L’Amour est dans le pré », qu’est-ce qui vous surprend encore dans cette émission ? Ce qui surprend, c’est l’humain. C’est ça qui est magnifique avec une émission comme ça. Chaque année est différente, chaque instant, chaque jour, chaque minute compte, parce que c’est de l’humain, et que l’humain est imprévisible. Donc on est surpris à chaque fois. Que nous réserve alors cette nouvelle saison ? Cette année encore, il y a eu de belles surprises. On est vraiment revenus à l’essence même de « L’Amour est dans le pré », avec tout ce qu’il y a de plus beau : les vraies valeurs, les bonnes et vraies raisons pour lesquelles les agriculteurs et agricultrices sont là. Il y a des histoires qui vont au-delà de la simple envie de trouver l’amour, des parcours très particuliers qui expliquent pourquoi l’amour a été difficile à trouver jusque-là. On va vraiment suivre tout un processus de vie au travers des émissions, qui aboutit souvent à de très jolies choses cette année. Y a-t-il eu des moments où vous vous êtes dit « zut, ça, je ne l’avais pas vu venir » ? Oui, ça, c’est un point commun à chaque année ! C’est vrai que l’on voit une histoire qui démarre d’une certaine manière, on se dit que ça va être presque comme d’habitude, et puis c’est tout le contraire que ce qu’on avait imaginé. Ce n’est pas plus mal d’avoir plein de moments où je me suis laissé surprendre. Vous connaissez bien la mécanique de l’émission, les humains et les relations amoureuses aussi. Sentez-vous assez vite quels couples ont une chance de perdurer et lesquels vont droit dans le mur ? Il y a des choses évidentes, comme lors de ma première saison avec Luc et Pauline. Là, franchement, on ne se pose même pas la question. Je crois que c’est encore le cas cette année, il y a une histoire d’amour assez frappante. Pour le reste, on a sa propre sensibilité, son regard un peu extérieur. Parfois je me dis que peut-être que j’aurais été plus dans ce sens-là que dans l’autre, mais je ne suis pas à la place de la personne, et mon rôle n’est certainement pas de l’influencer, parce que pour rien au monde je ne voudrais me tromper à ce niveau-là. Donc il faut laisser parler le cœur. Mais il y a parfois des choses qui semblaient assez évidentes sur le moment, et puis d’autres qui te surprennent sincèrement, où tu te dis « ah, je n’aurais pas vu ça comme ça ». Vous arrive-t-il de penser « non, surtout pas celle-là ou celui-là », ou d’imaginer votre choix vers quelqu’un d’autre ? Oui, dans mon esprit, dans ma tête, mais je ne le verbalise jamais ! Mais c’est vrai que de l’extérieur, je me dis parfois « ah, c’était plutôt lui ou elle ». Je suis aussi très attentive au speed dating, c’est là que le courant passe ou ne passe pas, et j’écoute un peu les réflexions de chacun. Et avant ça, je me suis beaucoup intéressée à l’agriculteur ou l’agricultrice, donc je sais ce qu’il ou elle a traversé, je sais pourquoi il ou elle est là, je sais ce qu’il ou elle cherche à ne pas reproduire. Mais je ne peux pas forcer la main en l’obligeant à choisir ce qui me semblait le meilleur choix ! Les agriculteurs qui participent aujourd’hui à l’émission sont-ils différents de ceux des premières saisons ? Sont-ils plus à l’aise avec les codes de la télé, les réseaux sociaux, leur image ? Ce n’est que ma troisième année, ça me permet d’évaluer la chose sur trois ans, mais en tout cas, on constate à chaque fois la même mécanique : ce sont des personnes qui arrivent fébriles, complètement vulnérables, un peu mal à l’aise face à la caméra. Et puis il y a une espèce de symbiose qui se crée. Ce qui est important, c’est de rappeler la bienveillance de toutes les personnes qui sont derrière les caméras, l’équipe de « L’Amour est dans le pré ». Ça ne pourrait pas fonctionner si les équipes n’étaient pas celles-là depuis si longtemps. Et au final, les agriculteurs et agricultrices se sentent comme dans une espèce de famille. Ils se sentent bien. Il y a une belle complicité qui se crée, à tel point que quand vient le moment de partir avec les équipes, ça crée un petit vide, et souvent il y a des larmes. Et le but, c’est de trouver l’amour – ils en arrivent à oublier les caméras pour se concentrer sur leur quête. Les oublient-ils réellement, ou est-ce une jolie légende de la télé ? Non, vraiment, on les sent portés par l’émotion. Je crois que c’est la force de « L’Amour est dans le pré », une émission qui est tout en confidences et en confiance. Quand on est bousculé, bouleversé par des émotions qui viennent de se passer suite à une rencontre, suite à quelque chose qui s’est bien ou moins bien passé, la personne oublie totalement, elle a juste besoin de se confier. En général, j’ai la chance d’être en face d’elle à ce moment-là, et elle a juste envie de parler, d’oublier. Un peu comme moi : moi aussi j’oublie beaucoup les caméras. Je suis une plaie pour les caméras, parce que je suis tellement dans l’instant face à la personne qui est avec moi que je ne me rends pas compte que je tourne le dos aux caméras, je ne suis pas au bon endroit. Tout simplement parce que je vis l’instant présent avec eux. On parle beaucoup de solitude dans le monde agricole. Avez-vous l’impression que la situation s’améliore ou cela reste-t-il un milieu assez solitaire ? Cela reste un métier vraiment solitaire. Au-delà de la solitude, c’est un métier qui demande une telle passion, un tel dévouement : il n’y a pas d’heure, on dépend des saisons, du rythme, des difficultés, de sa ferme… On est au rythme de son exploitation non-stop, la tête dans le guidon, et c’est souvent assez difficile de prendre le temps d’aller rencontrer quelqu’un. Une fois qu’on rencontre cette personne, encore faut-il qu’elle comprenne le rythme et l’investissement que ça demande. Il y a un amour tellement intense et profond pour le métier et pour leur ferme que tout ça, de manière insidieuse, provoque une certaine solitude. « L’Amour est dans le pré », dimanche, 19 h 30, RTL-TVi. Maria Del Rio a repris la route des fermes wallonnes pour aider les agriculteurs à trouver l’amour. Par Sophie Lagesse Journaliste Le 20/09/2026 à 08:00

Dernier jour des élections législatives en Russie : Moscou dénonce une attaque de drones REUTERS. L es Russes se rendent aux urnes dimanche pour le troisième et dernier jour d’élections législatives qui devraient sans surprise se solder par la victoire du parti de Vladimir Poutine, plus de quatre ans et demi après le début de la guerre en Ukraine. Ces législatives, les premières depuis le début de l’offensive à grande échelle contre l’Ukraine en 2022, visent à renouveler les 450 sièges de la Douma, la chambre basse du Parlement russe, et se déroulent aussi dans les territoires d’Ukraine occupés et annexés par la Russie. Rappelant la réalité d’un conflit marqué ces derniers mois par une intensification des frappes des deux côtés du front, le dernier jour de vote a été précédé dans la capitale russe par une attaque mobilisant des centaines de drones. Le gouverneur de la région entourant Moscou, Andreï Vorobiov, a fait état de 249 drones abattus par la défense anti-aérienne, touchant plusieurs zones résidentielles de la périphérie où deux morts ont été recensés. A Moscou même, une importante raffinerie a été endommagée, selon le maire Sergueï Sobianine. Ce dernier a dénoncé sur Telegram une attaque « sans précédent » et « manifestement planifiée dans le but de perturber les élections ». « L’ennemi n’y est pas parvenu », a-t-il ajouté, évoquant de son côté plus de 1.600 drones abattus par la défense anti-aérienne russe, dont « 450 se dirigeaient vers Moscou ». L’issue du scrutin fait peu de doutes L’issue du scrutin fait peu de doute dans un pays où l’expression de la dissidence est sévèrement réprimée par les autorités et alors que le seul parti frontalement opposé à la guerre, Iabloko, a été écarté. Les analystes scruteront malgré tout le taux de participation et les résultats des partis alternatifs pour sonder l’état d’esprit des Russes, confrontés à des sanctions économiques occidentales, des frappes ukrainiennes régulières, des pénuries d’essence et des limitations dans le fonctionnement de l’internet dans plusieurs régions. Face à Russie unie, le parti au pouvoir, seules des formations soutenant à des degrés divers Vladimir Poutine et la poursuite du conflit en Ukraine – les communistes du KPRF, les nationalistes du LDPR, les conservateurs de Russie juste et les libéraux du parti des Nouvelles personnes – ont été autorisées à concourir. À lire aussi Cinq années de correspondance en Russie, cinq années de durcissement accéléré Ecartée du scrutin, l’opposition en exil a appelé tous les « Russes opposés à la guerre » à voter contre le parti de Vladimir Poutine le même jour à la même heure, dimanche à midi, pour montrer leur nombre. L’Union européenne a de son côté dénoncé des élections se déroulant dans un climat de « répression systématique et institutionnalisée ». Le vote, qui a commencé vendredi matin, va durer jusqu’à 18 h GMT (20 h à Bruxelles) dimanche et les premiers résultats sont attendus dans la foulée. Cyberattaque Devant un théâtre moscovite, transformé en bureau de vote, en plein centre de la capitale russe, Tatiana, retraitée de 71 ans qui ne donne pas son nom, a dit samedi à l’AFP avoir voté pour Russie unie. « C’est le plus grand parti, le plus travailleur et qui a le plus de résultats », estime-t-elle. Diana, 30 ans, a donné pour sa part sa voix au parti des Nouvelles personnes, en espérant que cette formation accordera davantage d’attention aux problèmes économiques. « Beaucoup de gens ont perdu leur emploi. Les salaires sont désormais en baisse, et non plus en hausse », regrette-t-elle, affirmant par ailleurs vouloir la paix avec l’Ukraine. « Mais en regardant toute cette situation, il me semble que (la guerre) ne finira pas bientôt », ajoute la jeune femme qui a requis l’anonymat. À lire aussi Face aux rumeurs d’une nouvelle mobilisation, les Russes cherchent à s’échapper pour ne pas mourir Alors que le vote se déroule également électroniquement dans une trentaine de régions, la Commission électorale a fait état samedi d’une « cyberattaque très puissante » pour tenter de perturber le scrutin. Selon elle, « la situation est sous contrôle et la sécurité du système » est assurée. Elle a également rapporté que des lignes de communication dans l’Extrême-Orient russe avaient été sectionnées dans le même but. « Nous considérons cet incident comme un acte délibéré de sabotage », a déclaré Ella Pamfilova, présidente de la Commission électorale. Autre sujet qui pèse sur ces élections : la crainte d’une nouvelle mobilisation militaire sur le modèle de la « mobilisation partielle » de 300.000 réservistes en septembre 2022. Depuis que le président ukrainien Volodymyr Zelensky a affirmé qu’une telle mesure serait annoncée « à l’automne » après les législatives, son homologue russe et son entourage ont réfuté à de multiples reprises ce scénario, très impopulaire jusque dans les cercles dirigeants à Moscou. Les législatives visent à renouveler les 450 sièges de la Douma, la chambre basse du Parlement russe, et se déroulent aussi dans les territoires d’Ukraine occupés et annexés par la Russie. Sous pression américaine, la Turquie multiplie les mesures visant des intérêts iraniens. La Turquie a révoqué samedi 19 septembre la licence de la banque iranienne Mellat, une entité semi-privée visée depuis des années par des sanctions occidentales. Ce nouveau coup porté au système bancaire de Téhéran s’inscrit dans une série de mesures prises récemment par Ankara à l’encontre d’intérêts iraniens, sur fond de pression américaine croissante. Ces décisions coïncident également avec le déplacement du président turc Recep Tayyip Erdogan aux États-Unis, à l’occasion de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies la semaine prochaine.

Ouganda: Kampala suspend sa coopération militaire avec la Turquie. En Allemagne, deux élections régionales décisives pour l’avenir de Friedrich Merz. Il y a deux semaines, la victoire écrasante de l’extrême droite en Saxe-Anhalt secouait le pays. Le parti du chancelier Merz subissait une défaite cuisante. Ce dimanche, deux autres régions, le Mecklembourg et Berlin, votent. De mauvais résultats pour la CDU pourraient accélérer le calendrier politique alors que Friedrich Merz est sur la sellette.

Qui étaient les Dénisoviens?. C’est une première : de très rares fossiles de Dénisoviens, les énigmatiques « cousins » asiatiques de Néandertal, ont été mis au jour dans une grotte du sud-ouest de la Chine, aux côtés des outils en pierre dont ils se servaient. Une découverte exceptionnelle qui nous éclaire sur la vie quotidienne et les capacités de ces anciens humains aujourd’hui disparus.

How Americanness Overcomes Islamophobia. In Rozina Ali’s new book, four families grapple with the post-9/11 shift.
Emily Wilson Chooses Her Words Carefully. The Homeric scholar’s new book on translation is bitingly smart.
Chinese Literature Is Undergoing a Vibe Shift. Beijing long promoted novels about working-class travails. What happens when authors point fingers at the state?
In War, Trump and Putin Are Much Alike. Washington is emulating Moscow’s ways of fighting wars—and helping it in the process.
What in the World?. Test yourself on the week of Sept. 12: Modi and Xi meet, the Houthis fire on Saudi Arabia, and EU leaders gather in Finland.
Will Russia Ever Be ‘Normal’?. Empires inevitably decline, and Putin’s project will be no exception.
Russia’s Parliamentary Elections Offer Rituals, Not Results. Polling shows that United Russia is all but certain to maintain its power.

Second Sunni cleric killed in Iran in less than a week. Sunni Baluch cleric Molavi Yousef Gorgij was killed by unknown assailants outside his home in Zahedan, Iranian state media reported on Monday, the second killing of a Sunni cleric in Iran in less than a week.

Resistance born from Mahsa Amini’s death endures, UN rapporteur says. UN Special Rapporteur on Iran Mai Sato said the movement born from Mahsa “Jina” Amini’s death in Iran’s morality police custody remains alive four years on, despite another deadly crackdown and continued enforcement of mandatory hijab rules.

US sanctions Russia’s VTB Bank over Iran ties as financial crackdown widens. The United States on Monday imposed new Iran-related sanctions on Russia’s VTB Bank on Monday, accusing the already heavily sanctioned lender of helping Tehran evade restrictions through banking relationships and payment arrangements.

US, Iran hint at talks even as sanctions tighten and Hormuz tensions stay high. The United States and Iran both signaled openness to renewed negotiations Monday, even as Washington intensified its financial pressure campaign and conflicting accounts of incidents around the Strait of Hormuz underscored the mistrust surrounding any diplomatic opening.

Iran's Saudi leverage could become its liability. Iran has gained leverage over Saudi Arabia as Houthi advances and attacks put pressure on the kingdom’s territory and oil routes. But Riyadh is responding more forcefully, raising the risk that Tehran’s advantage could provoke a military backlash that ultimately weakens it.

Xi’s BRICS peace call sparks debate in Iran over China’s role in war. China’s call for a collective BRICS role in restoring peace in the Persian Gulf and Middle East has triggered debate in Iran over whether Beijing is preparing to mediate between Tehran and Washington.

US seeks $61 million in cryptocurrency tied to Iran oil sales. US prosecutors are seeking the forfeiture of about $61 million in cryptocurrency that came from black-market sales of sanctioned Iranian crude oil and petroleum products and was intended to finance Iran's government and military, including the Revolutionary Guards.

Iranian security forces arrest three Baha’is in Shiraz, source says. Iranian security forces arrested three Baha’i citizens during raids on their homes in Shiraz, southwestern Iran, on Monday and transferred them to an undisclosed location, Iran International has learned.

Islamic Republic asks public to identify opponents abroad. The Islamic Republic has launched a platform asking citizens to identify and report opponents living abroad. Iranians met it with ridicule, pointing to how deeply the state's own security apparatus has been infiltrated.

Women face forced undressing, breast touching at Iran's Evin Prison. Female political prisoners at Iran's Evin Prison face increasingly invasive body searches involving forced undressing and breast touching, leading some to forgo medical treatment and visits, sources told Iran International.

EU Parliament names Iran among states behind hybrid attacks on Europe. The European Parliament on Tuesday named Iran among countries it said were involved in hybrid attacks targeting Europe, including cyberattacks, sabotage, espionage and signal jamming.

Hormuz traffic plunges ahead of Iran-China talks. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz fell sharply as Iran prepared diplomatic talks in China, while attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to Persian Gulf cloud infrastructure underscored the widening consequences of the war on Tuesday.

After Muscat collapse, Tehran argues over what comes next. Iranian newspapers that agree on almost nothing agreed on Monday that the Muscat talks had collapsed. Kayhan, Shargh and Donya-ye Eghtesad all reported it, and the argument has already moved to what Tehran does next.

January's unfinished love stories: Lives severed by Iran protest killings. Eight months after Iran's January protests, the partners left behind by some of those killed are recounting lives abruptly divided by gunfire – marriages measured in months or days, anniversaries spent at graves and final embraces they never knew were their last.

Tehran political circles see US hand in postponement of Oman Hormuz talks. Iranian lawmakers, hardline media and analysts have blamed Washington for postponing Oman-hosted talks on Strait of Hormuz shipping arrangements, despite officials attributing the delay to regional objections and Saudi concerns over Yemen.

Iranian court upholds death sentence for another protest detainee. An Iranian appeals court has upheld the death sentence of Ali Rahimi Rigi, a 32-year-old detainee from the January protests, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

‘This is the cost you must pay’: Iran accused of denying food to death-row twin. Twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi have been tortured in detention and threatened with sexual violence, while death-row Taraneh is now being denied food in retaliation for family advocacy, their cousin told Iran International.

A generation shaped by Woman, Life, Freedom refuses to go back. Four years after Mahsa “Jina” Amini’s death in Iran’s morality police custody sparked the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, teenagers who watched her name become a rallying cry have grown up amid repression but beyond many of the social and political boundaries of pre-2022 Iran.

Security forces deploy as shops in western Iran strike on Mahsa Amini anniversary. Iranian security forces fanned out across several western cities on Wednesday as shopkeepers shut down businesses to mark the fourth anniversary of the death of Mahsa Amini, according to videos and messages sent to Iran International.

Iran used state machinery to crush 2022 uprising, Amnesty says. Iranian state authorities organized a systematic, high-level campaign of murder, torture, and sexual violence to crush the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, according to a 1,000-page investigation published by Amnesty International on Wednesday.

Shot and left for dead, Iran protester faces 26th surgery. Twenty-five surgeries have failed to end the ordeal of a protester shot during January demonstrations in Iran, with a severe infection still spreading through the wounded leg and a 26th operation now planned, Iran International learned.

US officials met Iran-aligned Houthis in Oman - Reuters. US officials met representatives of Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in Oman over the weekend, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing five sources familiar with the matter, days after the group seized a strategic stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast.

Iranian women recall the first time they went out uncovered. Four years after the Woman, Life, Freedom protests, Iran International asked women on Instagram to describe the first time they went out without a headscarf. The answers came back in the same four registers: fear, freedom, grief and solidarity.

Mahsa’s dandelion: step by step through Iran's Woman, Life, Freedom. Mahsa Amini’s death in September 2022 set off something that could not be put back in its box. Woman, Life, Freedom challenged the foundations of the Islamic Republic. This interactive project retraces the uprising, what was lost, but also what survived and what changed.

From Halkbank to Golden Global: Turkey’s Iran banking ties under US scrutiny. Turkey has stepped in to take control of shareholder rights at a bank accused by Washington of helping Tehran turn oil revenues into cash and gold: the latest chapter in a decades-long story linking Turkish banking, US sanctions and Iranian money.
Mahsa Amini and the century-long struggle of Iranian women. In September 2022, the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in the custody of Iran’s morality police ignited a fire that still burns.

Calls to quit NPT grow in Iran as critics warn of strategic trap. Calls for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty are gaining ground among hardliners after the IAEA referred the country to the UN Security Council and its nuclear chief was barred from attending the agency’s annual conference in Vienna.

Italian city dedicates riverside green space to Mahsa Amini. The Italian city of Imola has dedicated a green space to Mahsa Jina Amini, marking the fourth anniversary of her death in Iran’s morality-police custody and honoring the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising that followed, a Bologna-based daily newspaper reported.

UN says Iran crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity. Iranian security forces committed crimes against humanity in their crackdown on nationwide protests, a UN fact-finding mission said on Thursday, citing mass killings, torture and arbitrary detention.

Iran cancer patients sell household goods to pay for treatment. Some cancer patients in Iran are selling essential household goods or abandoning medication as soaring drug prices and gaps in insurance coverage put treatment beyond the reach of low-income families, a charity director said on Thursday.

US House passes Iran sanctions as Trump signals war may be nearing end. The US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, clearing the sweeping measure for President Donald Trump’s signature as Washington also signaled that the Iran war could be approaching a diplomatic turning point.

Video of Iran's police sexually abusing teenager draws fury. A video showing Iranian police beating and sexually humiliating a teenager while officers laugh, insult him and film the abuse has unleashed fury across Iranian social media, with users asking what may happen beyond public view.

Woman, Life, Freedom and the Iran that cannot go back. Four years after Mahsa Amini’s death, the deepest legacy of Woman, Life, Freedom may be that Iran cannot simply be returned to the society it was before September 2022.

Why Iran’s hardliners keep talking of ousting Pezeshkian. Renewed talk among Iranian hardliners of removing President Masoud Pezeshkian has revived comparisons with Iran’s only presidential impeachment, but there is little evidence so far of a coordinated effort capable of unseating him.

Iran rapidly rebuilding site tied to past nuclear weapons research - report. Iran is rapidly reconstructing a heavily fortified facility at the Parchin military complex that was previously linked to nuclear weapons research and has been struck twice since 2024, new satellite imagery analyzed by a Washington-based nuclear watchdog shows.

US offers substantial whistleblower rewards for tips on Iran sanction evasion. The US Treasury is offering whistleblowers up to 30% of collected penalties for information leading to enforcement actions over Iran-related sanctions evasion or money laundering, as Washington seeks intelligence on Tehran’s financial networks abroad.

Trump weighs major Iran escalation as China steps up diplomatic push. President Donald Trump said Thursday he was weighing renewed large-scale strikes on Iran as China intensified diplomatic contacts with Washington and Tehran amid mounting pressure to contain the regional conflict.

Iran’s nightly pro-state rallies become factional battleground. Iran’s nightly pro-government rallies have become an increasingly visible show of political force, occupying streets and squares for 200 consecutive nights and, more recently, turning their fire on rivals within the Islamic Republic itself.

Iranian protester, 21, dies after about 30 operations for gunshot wounds. A 21-year-old taekwondo athlete shot by Iranian security forces during January protests has died after undergoing about 30 operations, according to information received by Iran International.

Iran faces postwar winter with a third of gas capacity lost. Iran is racing to restore gas infrastructure before winter after losing about a third of its pre-war production capacity, a reconstruction challenge that could force Tehran into difficult choices between keeping homes warm, power plants running and industry supplied.

Iran's Guards stage show of force two days after protest anniversary. Iran's Revolutionary Guards paraded uniformed volunteers, Basij paramilitaries and children through Tehran on Friday in a state-organized show of force, two days after the anniversary of the 2022 protests.

Tehran ‘ashamed’ as Iranians struggle to make ends meet. Iran’s economic hardship has grown so acute that senior government officials are increasingly acknowledging in public the scale of the pressure on ordinary households.

Unveiled runners draw attention at Tehran 10k race. Videos showing women running without headscarves at a road race in Tehran went viral on Friday, months after a similar event on Kish Island prompted action against its organizers.

Democrats seize on Iran war costs to hit Trump ahead of midterms. Democrats are intensifying attacks on President Donald Trump over the Iran war as the midterm elections approach, seeking to tie the six-month conflict to an issue closer to American voters’ wallets: the rising cost of gasoline and everyday goods.

Tehran sees ‌Beijing as potential bridge to Washington. Iranian officials and media are increasingly looking to China as a possible diplomatic bridge to Washington, as Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s second wartime visit to Beijing coincides with preparations for President Xi Jinping’s talks with Donald Trump next week.

Death-row Iran protester denied hospital treatment, family says. An Iranian woman sentenced to death over January’s anti-government protests is struggling to walk but has been denied hospital treatment despite a prison doctor saying she urgently needs an MRI, her family told Iran International.

Iran executes man it accused of spying for Israel on missile sites. Iran has executed a man it accused of passing information about missile sites in Isfahan to Israel's Mossad, the judiciary said on Saturday, the latest in a series of espionage executions that rights groups say rest on confessions extracted in detention.

Iran sets seven terms for renewed US talks, says ready for escalation. Iran has conveyed seven conditions to Washington for the start of any negotiations, Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Saturday, as President Donald Trump weighs whether to resume major attacks on Iran.

Will shutdowns forced by US blockade damage Iran’s oil wells?. The sharp fall in Iran’s oil loadings is forcing it to curb production, raising costs beyond lost sales, from restarting aging wells to maintaining reservoir pressure and protecting shared fields. But could the shutdowns cause lasting damage?

Iran mobilisation drive extends to children under 15. The spokesman for Iran’s mass mobilisation campaign said children under 15 could be introduced to military concepts, while denying that minors were receiving formal weapons training as authorities expand a civilian defence drive launched during the war.

États-Unis-Mali : des élus américains demandent un encadrement du rapprochement Trump-Goïta. Face à la propagation du Jnim au Sahel, des élus républicains et démocrates américains veulent encadrer le rapprochement entre l’administration Trump et le Mali. Un projet de loi bipartisan exige une stratégie diplomatique transparente pour contrer l’expansion jihadiste.

Pourquoi l’échec de Drapor pèse toujours sur la souveraineté économique du Maroc. Longtemps symbole de souveraineté industrielle du royaume, la société spécialisée dans le dragage incarne désormais un des échecs retentissants de la politique de privatisation des années 1990. Un dossier qui a encore des répercussions aujourd’hui.

Le chanteur marocain Saad Lamjarred jugé en appel en France pour viol. Le chanteur marocain Saad Lamjarred, condamné à six ans de prison pour viol et violences aggravées, est jugé en appel à partir du 17 septembre à Créteil. Il comparaîtra libre sous contrôle judiciaire.

Jeune Afrique réagit au retrait de l’accréditation de son correspondant en Guinée. Le 16 septembre, la Haute Autorité de la communication (HAC) guinéenne a rendu publique une décision de retrait de l’accréditation de notre correspondant en Guinée, Diawo Barry. Jeune Afrique réagit.

10 choses à savoir sur Tchakpelé Aklesso, l’ancien maître espion nommé par Faure Gnassingbé à la tête de l’armée togolaise. Promu général et chef d’état-major, Tchakpelé Aklesso incarne la nouvelle doctrine sécuritaire de Faure Gnassingbé. Portrait d’un homme de l’ombre propulsé à la tête d’une armée en pleine mutation.

Gabon : tout comprendre au tour de passe-passe de Libreville pour se désendetter. Le nouvel inventaire des engagements publics donne à Libreville une base comptable plus précise pour piloter ses finances. Un ajustement qui intervient alors que le pays cherche à stabiliser ses comptes et à avancer dans ses discussions avec le FMI.

Comment l’ivoirien Yeshi veut accélérer au Cameroun. Le groupe Yeshi, connu pour sa filiale de matériaux de construction et de quincaillerie Bernabé, mise sur son expérience en Côte d’Ivoire, au Sénégal et au Gabon pour assurer son essor au Cameroun. Il parie sur le secteur automobile.

Comment le PAPSS d’Afreximbank veut connecter l’Afrique au reste du monde. Créé pour fluidifier les paiements intra-africains, le PAPSS franchit une nouvelle étape en s’ouvrant aux grandes puissances commerciales mondiales. La plateforme vise également l’interopérabilité des cartes bancaires à travers le continent.

Rwanda-Bénin : chez Paul Kagame, les dossiers très sécuritaires de Romuald Wadagni. Avant Brazzaville, où il est arrivé ce 17 septembre, le président béninois a effectué une visite officielle à Kigali. Au cœur des discussions avec son homologue rwandais, le renforcement du partenariat sur les questions militaires et de renseignements.

Côte d’Ivoire : la justice allège les charges contre Blaise Lasm, proche de Laurent Gbagbo. Détenu depuis septembre 2025, le responsable du PPA-CI a obtenu un non-lieu partiel. Son dossier est désormais renvoyé devant le tribunal correctionnel.

Cameroun : dans les coulisses d’un renseignement d’État privatisé. Officiellement destinés à protéger l’État, les services de renseignement du Cameroun, précarisés, se mettent régulièrement au service d’intérêts privés contre rémunération. Plongée au cœur du marché noir des informations.

Niger : dans la tête d’Abdourahamane Tiani, président retranché. Après la mutinerie du 29 août, le chef de la junte semble plus isolé que jamais. Il se méfie de son armée, et ne fait plus confiance qu’à sa Garde présidentielle, à une poignée d’officiers encore fidèles et à ses alliés russes et algériens.

Après l’Algérie, la Tunisie de Kaïs Saïed déclare la guerre au narcotrafic. Quelques jours après le voisin algérien, la Tunisie annonce à son tour vouloir renforcer la lutte contre les réseaux de trafic de stupéfiants. Dans les deux pays, les quantités saisies et la consommation ont explosé ces dernières années.

Au Maroc, l’héritage bénéfique de la crise de la BNDE. Après avoir servi de bras armé du royaume en matière de financement de l’industrie, la BNDE a été liquidée au milieu des années 2000 sur fond de scandale financier. Ce dossier a conduit à un renforcement de la régulation bancaire au Maroc.

Déguerpissements en Côte d’Ivoire : le gouverneur d’Abidjan, Ibrahim Cissé Bacongo, fragilisé. Les révélations du procureur sur le rôle d’Ibrahim Cissé Bacongo dans la destruction de 250 logements à Koumassi affaiblissent le secrétaire exécutif du parti présidentiel. Elles questionnent aussi l’encadrement de ces opérations de démolition qui se sont multipliées à Abidjan.

Finale de la Coupe du monde 2030 : face aux ambitions du Maroc, l’Espagne menace. Depuis l’attribution du tournoi 2030 au trio Maroc-Portugal-Espagne, la question de savoir quel pays accueillera la finale oppose Madrid et Rabat. Une rivalité envenimée par la crise de Ceuta et la dégradation de leurs relations diplomatiques.

Mark Suzman (Fondation Gates) : « L’IA peut permettre d’atteindre les objectifs de développement du continent ». Le PDG de la Fondation Gates alerte sur les conséquences de la baisse de l’aide publique au développement. Et parie sur l’intelligence artificielle pour lutter contre la pauvreté, les maladies et améliorer l’éducation.

Ambassades et liaisons aériennes : à New York, le Maroc et Israël renforcent leurs liens. Lors d’une rencontre à trois incluant l’ambassadeur américain aux Nations unies, les ministres marocain et israélien des Affaires étrangères ont notamment décidé de transformer leurs représentations diplomatiques en véritables ambassades.

Transport maritime : Hapag-Lloyd et DP World, la revanche africaine des outsiders. Le cinquième armateur mondial et l’opérateur portuaire émirati scellent une collaboration sur le long terme dans cinq ports africains, qui doit apporter un peu plus de visibilité au premier et de respectabilité au second.

Niger : qui sont les personnalités déchues de leur nationalité par Abdourahamane Tiani ?. Le chef de la junte a déchu provisoirement de leur nationalité cinq de ses compatriotes, parmi lesquels plusieurs anciens responsables du régime de Mohamed Bazoum. Une mesure qui intervient moins de trois semaines après les événements du 29 août à Niamey.

Les marchés de capitaux, grands gagnants de l’IPO Dangote. Avec l’entrée en Bourse de sa raffinerie, Dangote entend mettre les épargnants nigérians au cœur de l’essor industriel du pays. Mais l’opération teste aussi la capacité du Nigeria à faire de Lagos une place financière de premier plan.

Au Sénégal, Bassirou Diomaye Faye cultive le mystère autour des élections locales. La confusion règne autour du calendrier des élections municipales et départementales initialement prévues en janvier 2027, qui seront probablement reportées sans que Bassirou Diomaye Faye ne s’en soit jusqu’à présent expliqué. Alors qu’il ne bénéficie plus du soutien de Pastef, le chef de l’État appréhenderait-il cette confrontation électorale à haut risque au point de chercher à l’ajourner ?

En RDC, l’ancien ministre Constant Mutamba poursuit sa dégringolade. Déjà condamné à trois ans de travaux forcés, en septembre 2025, l’ex-ministre de la Justice a été reconnu coupable de détournement de fonds destinés à l’indemnisation des victimes de la guerre de Kisangani. Il écope cette fois d’une peine de dix ans de prison et poursuit sa chute spectaculaire, un an après sa démission du gouvernement.

Guerre des drones au Mali, interview exclusive de Fouzi Lekjaâ, les secrets du renseignement camerounais… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique enquête sur les victimes civiles des frappes de drones au Mali, revient sur les ambitions politiques de Fouzi Lekjaâ au Maroc, dévoile les dessous de la guerre des clans qui fragilise les services de renseignements camerounais, décrypte les affrontements entre opposition et partisans du pouvoir en RDC et analyse les conséquences de la faillite de la Samir sur la politique énergétique marocaine.

Alliés lointains, voisins hostiles : en Éthiopie, le pari diplomatique à haut risque d’Abiy Ahmed. Addis-Abeba cultive l’art des alliances transversales, séduisant simultanément l’Occident, la Chine et les pays du Golfe. Une agilité qui trouve ses limites face aux rivalités de la Corne de l’Afrique.

Après la rupture, Alger en dit plus sur les « ingérences » reprochées aux Émirats arabes unis. Pour justifier sa rupture diplomatique avec Abou Dhabi, Alger a notamment mis en avant des « ingérences » émiraties dans sa vie politique. Selon certaines sources, les soupçons portent sur des tentatives d’empêcher la victoire d’Abdelmadjid Tebboune aux présidentielles de 2019 et de 2024.

Secrétariat général de l’ONU : un troisième vote défavorable à Macky Sall. Au terme du troisième « straw poll » tenu au sein du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies vendredi 18 septembre, l’ex-président sénégalais accuse un net recul dans la course à la succession d’António Guterres.

Minerais critiques en RDC : des acteurs chinois toujours plus présents… et nombreux. Les entreprises de l’empire du Milieu sont désormais parties prenantes dans 49 projets miniers critiques en RDC. Un chiffre inédit.

Centrafrique : Hassan Bouba, l’ex-rebelle que Touadéra ne veut pas écarter. De Berbérati à Birao, l’ancien rebelle continue de s’afficher en homme de terrain. Passé à l’Urbanisme lors du dernier remaniement, le ministre reste un élément-clé des dossiers sécuritaires, en particulier depuis l’offensive sur Amdafok.

Comment Ceuta nourrit le discours de l’extrême droite européenne. La ruée vers Ceuta de dizaines de milliers de Marocains fin juillet a mis le feu aux poudres en Europe. Pour François Soudan, qui commente au micro de RFI l’article de notre collaboratrice Nina Kozlowski, ce « scénario idéal » profite avant tout aux droites identitaires occidentales.

Ebola en RDC : des « signes encourageants » dans la lutte contre l’épidémie, qui « continue de progresser et de tuer », déclare l’OMS. Le directeur général de l’organisation, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, a annoncé mercredi que les essais cliniques sur les traitements et les vaccins contre la maladie à virus s’accéléraient, alors que la RDC connaît la pire flambée de son histoire.

Soudan : au moins 82 morts dans l’effondrement d’une mine d’or. La mine d’Al-Zaraa s’est effondrée mardi, et « un nombre indéterminé » de personnes restent coincées sous les décombres, a déclaré, mercredi, une source des Forces de soutien rapide à l’Agence France-Presse.

En Algérie, l’enseignement du français en primaire relégué au second plan au profit de l’anglais. La réforme portée par le ministre de l’éducation a suscité une levée de boucliers dans les milieux francophones. Mais elle est soutenue par les partisans d’une mise à jour du système éducatif algérien.

Israël et le Maroc vont ouvrir des ambassades dans leurs pays respectifs, annonce la diplomatie de l’Etat hébreu. Le ministère israélien a aussi annoncé que des accords économiques seraient conclus entre les deux pays, qui disposent de bureaux de liaison, avant la fin de 2026, ainsi qu’une extension des vols directs entre le Maroc et Israël.

Dans le sud de l’Angola, le spectre d’une nouvelle sécheresse sous l’effet du « Super El Niño ». Depuis une dizaine d’années, l’Afrique australe est aux premières loges du dérèglement climatique. La situation pourrait encore s’aggraver avec le phénomène océanographique qui trouve son origine dans le Pacifique sud.

« Oui à l’excision » : la poussée réactionnaire qui secoue l’Afrique de l’Ouest. Portée par des campagnes virales et des relais d’opinion, la défense de l’excision gagne du terrain en Afrique de l’Ouest. Une résurgence des discours conservateurs qui fragilise des décennies de lutte contre les mutilations génitales féminines.

Du gouvernement à l’armée, le général Tiani resserre les rangs après la tentative de putsch au Niger. Depuis le 29 août, le chef de la junte a remplacé quatre ministres, démis de ses fonctions le chef d’état-major des armées et procédé à l’arrestation d’au moins 200 militaires.

En Guinée, la chaîne France 24 interdite de diffusion après qu’un présentateur a qualifié le chef de l’Etat, Mamadi Doumbouya, de « président putschiste ». Depuis l’arrivée au pouvoir du général Doumbouya, les principaux partis politiques ont été dissous, les manifestations, interdites, sont réprimées et de nombreux dissidents ont été arrêtés, condamnés, poussés à l’exil ou sont portés disparus.

Excision : la poussée réactionnaire qui secoue l’Afrique de l’Ouest. En 2023, une étude publiée dans la revue Nature, estimait que l’ablation partielle ou totale du clitoris, des petites ou des grandes lèvres ou encore l’infibulation – les différentes formes de l’excision –, causaient environ 44 000 décès par an dans quinze pays africains, dont le Mali.

De Sidiki Diabaté à Sona Jobarteh, un nouveau souffle pour la kora. L’instrument à cordes ouest-africain voit son public rajeunir et son répertoire évoluer, comme l’illustre le concert parisien du musicien malien, qui se produit vendredi 18 septembre à l’Accor Arena, la salle parisienne de 20 000 places.

Nigeria : enquête après la mort en détention de 37 hommes soupçonnés d’être des mineurs illégaux. Le gouverneur de l’Etat du Niger, dans le centre du pays, où affluent des milliers de chercheurs d’or artisanaux, a décrété trois jours de deuil et reporté le début de la campagne pour les élections prévues en janvier.

Des affrontements interethniques font 26 morts dans la région d’Abyei, que se disputent les deux Soudans. Des assassinats au sein de deux ethnies ont « exacerbé les tensions entre les deux communautés », a affirmé la mission de maintien de la paix de l’ONU pour ce territoire.

Au Maghreb, des fractures géopolitiques de plus en plus inquiétantes. La rivalité s’exacerbe entre le Maroc et l’Algérie, qui investissent massivement dans leur armement. Ce duel se prolonge au Sahel et ce alors que les tensions hispano-marocaines autour de Ceuta alourdissent davantage le climat régional.

L’expulsion « en urgence absolue » de l’influenceur algérien « Doualemn » annulée par le tribunal administratif de Paris. Le tribunal ne s’étant pas prononcé sur la demande d’annulation d’un second arrêté d’expulsion qui n’invoquait pas l’urgence absolue, l’influenceur algérien peut toujours être potentiellement renvoyé de France.

Dans le centre du Mali, les djihadistes du GSIM relancent des offensives d’envergure. Trois attaques importantes d’installations militaires, intervenues coup sur coup, confirment le danger que fait peser la franchise sahélienne d’Al-Qaida sur la junte de Bamako.

L’ouverture conjointe d’ambassades au Maroc et en Israël, une annonce historique contestée dans le royaume. Turkish foreign minister says Israel should not 'chase empty dreams' Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus has accused Israel of seeking to deepen divisions across the Middle East in its pursuit for a 'promised land'. “Israel should not chase empty dreams,” Kurtulmus said during a civil society gathering in Kirsehir, according to Al Jazeera. “Israel’s main goal is for the peoples of this region to fall out with each other, to fight each other, and to realise its own ‘promised land’,” he added. Ed Sheeran says what is happening in Gaza is 'catastrophic, unjustifiable' Pop Star Ed Sheeran has said what is happening in Gaza is “catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate” as he opened his solo concert in the US city of Philadelphia. Sheeran also said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine,” describing the suffering caused by the war as a “human tragedy,” while explaining that he has generally sought to keep his concerts focused on “unity, joy, escapism, love” rather than his own political views. It was Sheeran's first show since he dropped US rapper Macklemore from his US tour after Macklemore called for a “Free Palestine”. Sheeran said he could not keep Macklemore after stadium owners refused to let him perform. Sheeran drew flak for the move and his opening acts and his own band have quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. “I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division,” he said. “But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore. What happened in Israel and at the Nome Museum Festival on 7 Oct was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain," he said. "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate. Our hearts can be broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’s lives, children’s lives and the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.” Pro-Palestinian protesters rallied outside Lincoln Financial Field ahead of Ed Sheeran’s concert. Poll: US Jewish voters concerned Netanyahu policies fueling antisemitism A majority of American Jewish voters say they are deeply concerned that Israel’s actions under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have contributed to rising antisemitism and anti-Israel sentiment in the United States, even as an overwhelming majority continue to identify as pro-Israel, according to a new poll released this week. The survey, conducted by the Mellman Group for the Jewish Electorate Institute and published Thursday, found that 56 percent of respondents had a “great deal” of concern that “Israel’s actions under Netanyahu have increased antisemitism and anti-Israel sentiment in the US”. The view varied sharply by political affiliation, with 65 percent of Jewish Democrats expressing a high level of concern, compared with 46 percent of independents and 34 percent of Republicans. Other Findings: *Eighty-six percent of those surveyed described themselves as pro-Israel, while 65 percent of them said they were pro-Israel while critical of some or many Israeli government policies. *Seventy-one percent viewed Israel favourably, compared with 25 percent who viewed it unfavourably. *Sixty-one percent viewed Netanyahu unfavourably and 34 percent favourably; 67 percent wanted to see him replaced in Israel’s upcoming election. US military aid Fifty-two percent favoured either cutting or ending the aid to Israel, including 36 percent who supported reducing it and 17 percent who favoured eliminating the $3.3 billion in military assistance. Forty percent wanted funding maintained at its current level. Views of AIPAC and primary spending Fifty-one percent said they had heard at least something about pro-Israel involvement in this year’s primary races, up from 38 percent in March. Thirty-nine percent supported such activity, while 35 percent opposed it and 26 percent were unsure. Forty-two percent viewed the organisation favourably and 35 percent unfavourably, with 24 percent unsure.

Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei has said that Iran will not abandon its right to be present in the UN General Assembly, stressing that attending the UN meeting is not a privilege given by Washington, according to IRNA. Speaking in a televised programme, Baghaei said that being in New York held absolutely no charm for Iranian representatives, but it was a "trench that must not be abandoned". He added that the US "used every tool to prevent the Iranian delegation’s participation, ranging from derogatory remarks and media propaganda to abusing its commitments as the host government by creating delays or refusing to issue visas for several delegation members", IRNA reported.

Security forces kill 11 terrorists during operations in Balochistan's Panjgur, Chagai. Security forces have killed 11 terrorists in separate operations in Panjgur and Chagai districts of Balochistan, state broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported on Saturday, citing security sources. The operations were conducted under Operation Raddul Fitna 3 . In Panjgur’s Gowargo area, security forces neutralised five terrorists and recovered a large quantity of weapons and ammunition from their possession, according to the report. Meanwhile, six terrorists were killed during operations in the Aminabad and Siah Chang areas of Chagai district, it added. A significant cache of arms and explosive material was also seized during the operations. According to state-run APP , Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised the security forces for their successful operations against terrorists. The interior minister said the “security forces had once again thwarted the intentions of terrorists through effective action”. The actions carried out by the security forces reflected their commitment to safeguarding national security, Naqvi was quoted as saying. He said the successful operations demonstrated the forces’ resolve to confront threats and maintain stability. Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in recent weeks, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to a monthly assessment by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, terrorists of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in the Pishin district. In retaliatory action, security forces killed 10 terrorists while two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, according to the military’s media affairs wing. Also on August 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were killed following an intense exchange of fire. On September 2, security forces killed 12 terrorists in the Kalat district during an intelligence-based operation (IBO). Days later, the troops killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives during separate IBOs in Kharan and Washuk districts. Another 36 terrorists were eliminated during multiple “high-tempo” operations conducted in Mastung, Quetta, Kalat and Sibi districts, the Inter-Services Public Relations said on September 4. These also included thwarting an attack on a police station in Sibi’s Bhag area. On Thursday, seven terrorists were killed by security forces in an IBO in the Badrang area of Balochistan’s Awaran district. On Friday, security forces killed seven terrorists during two IBOs in the province’s Panjgur and Kachhi districts.

Trump says Denmark to give US 'permanent control' over Greenland security. Denmark on Saturday hailed a “binding” deal announced by United States President Donald Trump to give Washington “permanent control” over Greenland’s security and bar Russian and Chinese bases from the Arctic territory. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming Nato ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance. Denmark and Greenland — an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen — both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said on Saturday that the potential signing meant “next week could be a good week”. “A long period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic,” the foreign minister said in a social media post. He added that the deal, which he said respected Denmark’s “red lines”, was “important” in light of a changed security situation. But the terms of the deal are uncertain, and Denmark maintains its sovereignty remains intact. Permanent control In a statement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as “an agreement which at the same time recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.” The 80-year-old said it was an “‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!” and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory. Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic unfolds, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so. “This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” a State Department official said. At the Davos economic forum this past January, Trump reached a purported deal with Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague. Frederiksen said on Friday she was “pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” adding that it was “good for Nato and Europe”. Greenland PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the US “strengthens” the territory’s security. Nato tensions Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal. But several media outlets have reported that the US wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory. A 1951 defence pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island, provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance. At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and Nato. Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, Nato launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Dar stresses importance of uninterrupted energy supplies in phone call with Iran's FM Araghchi. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar stressed the importance of “uninterrupted energy supplies” and the “safe and expeditious passage of ships” during a conversation with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday, the Foreign Office (FO) said. In a post on X, FO said the deputy premier and the top Iranian diplomat discussed the latest regional developments. Dar “stressed the importance of uninterrupted energy supplies and the safe and expeditious passage of ships, particularly given their implications for developing countries and global supply chains”. He underscored that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means to ensure peace and stability in the region”, the statement added. The two agreed to maintain close cooperation and meet in New York on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly next week , according to FO. The phone call came amid concerns over disruptions to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab , two key maritime routes for global trade and energy supplies. Iran’s stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz since the US launched its war on February 28 has already impacted oil exports from the Middle East. Fears of worsening disruption have intensified after the Houthis seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab strait a week ago, declaring a maritime blockade on Riyadh. While the current blockade is limited to Saudi ships, fears of a wider closure persist. On Friday, Pakistan condemned Houthi attacks on merchant shipping in Bab al-Mandab and called for their immediate cessation. Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad said that disruptions and attacks on merchant vessels could have implications far beyond the affected regions, including by affecting energy prices and global food security. Ambassador Asim also linked Pakistan’s position on maritime security to its diplomatic efforts following the outbreak of hostilities between Iran and the United States. “Guided by these foundational principles, Pakistan acted as a mediator between Iran and the United States, following the outbreak of hostilities between the two countries,” he said. Last week, FO described the situation around the Bab al-Mandab Strait as “ exceptionally serious ” and said Islamabad was concerned about the widening conflict and its implications for regional stability and maritime security. It called for the Houthi conflict to be addressed through “dialogue and diplomacy, and not through coercive measures”. Meanwhile, Iran’s interior ministry said on Saturday that efforts were under way to resolve outstanding issues and return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed between Tehran and Washington in June. Ministry spokesperson Ali Zeynivand said Iran demands that “the other party adhere to its commitments in this agreement”, according to Al Jazeera , which cited the semi-official Tasnim news agency. The fragile ceasefire had collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, with the US and Iran trading strikes for 13 consecutive days .

DPM Dar directs inclusion of all operational fuel stations in PM’s relief scheme. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday directed that all operational fuel stations be brought onto the system under the prime minister’s fuel relief scheme , while permanently closed stations and those dealing exclusively in diesel be removed from the list. He issued the directives while chairing a meeting of the National Steering Committee on Fuel Subsidy to review the implementation of the scheme, according to a statement issued by his office. “Every fuel station which is open and operating” should be brought onto the system, while stations found permanently closed or dealing exclusively in diesel should be identified and removed from the list, the statement quoted him as saying. The committee was informed that an overwhelming majority of fuel stations across the country were now operational on the system and that citizens were redeeming fuel tokens. Registration is continuing nationwide via SMS to 9771. The committee also approved the redemption of fuel tokens via SMS at stations in areas without internet connectivity. Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) and the provinces were asked to furnish lists of such stations so that they could be brought onto the scheme without delay. The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) informed the committee that all payment claims received over the past three days had been settled in full, with claims received each day processed on the same day. Dar appreciated the efforts of the provincial administrations and the cooperation extended by the SBP, stressing that “the relief must continue to reach the intended beneficiaries without hindrance”. PM Shehbaz on Sep 13 announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Under the scheme, owners of motorcycles, rickshaws, Qingqis, three-wheelers and vehicles with engines of up to 800cc will receive a Rs100 per litre relief on petrol. On Friday, PM Shehbaz approved a revised structure for the public under the fuel relief scheme currently in vogue across the country, expanding it to include more two- and three-wheelers, and easing weekly limits to offer motorists more flexibility in how they use the support. He directed that motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqi rickshaws up to 20 years old should also be included in the scheme. Renewed hostilities in the Middle East, which have resulted in disruption of major oil supply routes, have caused fuel prices to rise in the past two months. In addition to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz due to the US-Iran war, trade via Bab al-Mandab — which has become a vital route for Saudi oil exports in recent months — is also facing a rising threat from Houthi rebels. The subsidy scheme faced snags on Thursday, the first day of its nationwide rollout, as many petrol pumps declined to honour the digital app, claiming they lacked the system needed to provide petrol at Rs100 per litre less. Amid the fuel crisis, the federal government on Thursday also reintroduced austerity measures, including setting 9pm as the closing time for markets and reducing fuel provision for official vehicles by 50 per cent for a period of three months.

LHC directs foreign ministry to process pleas over detention of 2 PTI-linked Pakistanis in UAE. The Lahore High Court (LHC) has directed the secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) to process and decide within 15 days representations concerning the detention of two Pakistani citizens and PTI-affiliated individuals in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Justice Sadiq Mahmud Khurram issued the directions in written orders on Sept 14 on two separate petitions filed by the families of Syed Salman Raza Zaidi and Muhammad Junaid Jahangir through Barrister Abuzar Salman Niazi. According to the petitions, Zaidi went missing from his residence in Sharjah on Sept 27, 2024, and was subsequently taken into custody by UAE authorities. His wife, Faryal Zainab, told the court that despite nearly two years having passed, she had not been provided with clear information about the charges against her husband, the judicial proceedings, any sentence imposed on him or the complete court record. In the second petition, Muhammad Ibrahim, Jahangir’s father, said his son was allegedly detained at Dubai airport on Sept 24, 2024, upon his return from Saudi Arabia. The petitions challenged the alleged failure of the federal government and the Foreign Office to provide effective consular protection and legal assistance to the two men. Barrister Niazi told the court that representations regarding the detention of both citizens had been submitted to the foreign secretary but had not been processed. The petitioners sought legal and consular assistance for the two men, access to their judicial records and diplomatic steps for their return to Pakistan. They also sought a report on the steps taken by the state in the matter. After examining the petitions and the documents attached to them, Justice Khurram directed the foreign secretary to process the representations concerning the detention of Zaidi and Jahangir in the UAE, if they were still pending, in accordance with the law and expeditiously. The court directed that the representations be decided preferably within 15 days of receipt of a certified copy of its orders. The judge disposed of both petitions with these directions.

Candidates from PML-N, PPP file papers for presidential election in AJK. MUZAFFARABAD: The ruling PML-N and opposition PPP on Saturday submitted nomination papers for their respective candidates for the office of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) president, setting the stage for a contest on September 24. The office of the AJK president has remained vacant since January this year following the death of Barrister Sultan Mahmood. Previously, then-Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar was serving as acting president. The role was then assumed by incumbent Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Tariq Farooq after he was elected speaker on August 25. Under the AJK Constitution, the president is elected by members of the Legislative Assembly by a majority of the total membership, in the manner prescribed by law. The nomination papers were received by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Justice (retd) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal, who is also the returning officer for the presidential election. The PML-N has fielded 62-year-old former minister Dr Najeeb Naqi, whose nomination was proposed by senior PML-N leader and former prime minister Raja Farooq Haider and seconded by AJK Prime Minister Iftikhar Gillani. Meanwhile, the PPP nominated 78-year-old Akbar for the office, with his nomination proposed by former minister Deevan Ali Khan Chughtai and seconded by fellow legislator Sardar Mukhtar Ahmed Abbasi. The PML-N hopeful arrived at the Election Commission office accompanied by his proposer and seconder, as well as several other PML-N legislators, including the party’s regional president, Shah Ghulam Qadir. Haider and Gillani first posed for photographs with the nomination paper as they appeared to formally hand it over to the CEC. Subsequently, several other PML-N legislators, including the party president and ministers, also posed with the same nomination paper, standing alongside the CEC and appearing to hand it over to him in a similar manner. Akbar was also accompanied by several PPP legislators, who posed for photographs during the submission of his nomination papers. Both nomination papers were declared valid after scrutiny. Candidates may withdraw their nomination papers by 11:30am on Sept 23 (Wednesday), while polling will be held at the AJK Assembly Secretariat from 10am to 1pm on Sept 24 (Thursday), followed by the counting of votes and announcement of the result on the same day. Last month, polls were held across the region for seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly. The elections in the region, originally scheduled for July 27, were divided into phases over security concerns amid unrest in the region. The first phase was held on July 27, the second on Aug 2 and the third on Aug 10. The third phase was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division, which comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli because of concerns over the law and order situation. In the direct elections to 38 constituencies, the PML-N secured 25 seats while the PPP won 12. The lone MLA-elect of the Awami Dast-o-Bazu party also joined hands with the PML-N . The PPP alleged widespread rigging in the polls, with the party also ramping up its criticism of the ruling PML-N. On August 24, the PML-N bagged five seats while the PPP won two of the seven reserved seats that were up for grabs in the assembly. Newly elected members of the AJK Legislative Assembly were administered the oath of office by Akbar that same day.

337,000 pensioners obtain proof of life certificates in a month. ISLAMABAD: More than 337,000 pensioners have obtained their Proof of Life certificate since its launch by the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) on August 20, 2026, according to official data. The certificate is an official document that verifies that a pensioner is alive. Giving a breakdown of the facility’s usage, Nadra said 174,906 pensioners (52 per cent) obtained the certificate through the Pak ID app from home, 134,521 (40pc) through Nadra Registration Centres, 24,248 (7pc) through e-Sahulat centres and 3,585 (1pc) through mobile registration vans. Pensioners can obtain the certificate online or at the nearest Nadra service channel, according to their convenience, for proof of life, it added. Nadra noted that certain elements were deliberately misleading pensioners and urged them not to pay heed to such rumours. Pensioners were urged to contact the Nadra helpline, their nearest Nadra office or an e-Sahulat centre in case of complaints. It added that if a CNIC number was not included in the list of pensioners, the relevant department should be contacted. On August 20, Nadra had made the Proof of Life Certificate free for pensioners and expanded access to the document through multiple channels across the country. The initiative was launched on the special directives of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in coordination with the Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Defence, Controller General of Accounts (CGA) and Military Accountant General (MAG). According to Nadra, the easiest option to obtain the certificate was through the PakID mobile application, through which eligible pensioners could obtain the certificate digitally from home. An immediate family member could also obtain the certificate on a pensioner’s behalf through their own PakID account, subject to the prescribed identity verification process. For those preferring assisted services, the certificate could be obtained free of charge at more than 5,000 e-Sahulat franchises and over 988 Nadra Registration Centres and 500 Union Councils, where pensioners are given preferential service without having to wait in the regular queue. For pensioners unable to reach a service point, Nadra said the facility was also available through mobile registration vans, biker services and ManPack registration services, which cater to citizens with limited mobility or access. The Proof of Life certificate service is part of a wider reform under which Nadra has established a National Pensioners Register. In Phase I, pensioners administered by CGA and MAG have been brought onto the register to provide an authenticated digital reference for identity and life-status verification. A separate verification service was made available to banks, allowing authorised banks to check a pensioner’s proof-of-life status directly through the National Pensioners Register. Nadra said this would provide a digital channel for pension disbursement and reduce reliance on repeated physical or paper-based verification. The authority expected the register to be expanded in the next phase to include pensioners from other federal and provincial government organisations, public-sector bodies and private institutions, after agreements and institutional arrangements had been concluded.

'No one can minus Imran': Senate opp leader says only PTI founder can postpone Sept 27 Islamabad march. Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas on Saturday said only PTI founder Imran Khan had the authority to postpone his party’s countrywide protest planned for September 27. The PTI has called for a nationwide protest , including a “ long march ” to Islamabad, to demand the release of party founder Imran Khan and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) opposition alliance, which Abbas is a key leader of, has assured the PTI of its support for the protest. A post on Abbas’ X account on Saturday claimed that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had called on him and that the latter was informed only Imran could postpone the September 27 protest. “No one can minus Imran,” he wrote. TTAP Spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousufzai, speaking to Dawn , claimed that the meeting was held on September 14 on Naqvi’s request. He added that Abbas and PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan attended the meeting on the opposition’s side. Responding to queries after a press conference at Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in Islamabad, Abbas said: “He (Naqvi) came to meet [us]. We have stated our stance and they will find out … that no individual can postpone the September 27 march without a meeting with Imran Khan sahib .” He asserted, “Imran Khan cannot be minused; we will not let Imran Khan sahib be minused. Therefore, no issue can be resolved without a meeting with Imran Khan sahib .” During the press conference, Abbas said providing basic facilities to the people and protecting their constitutional rights were major issues. He said that even a senior federal minister had acknowledged that the country’s system had “collapsed”. TTAP leader and former Sindh governor Mohammad Zubair said there was a wide gap between the lifestyle of the ruling elite and the economic difficulties faced by ordinary citizens. He claimed that poverty, unemployment and inflation had increased compared with four and a half years ago. He said electricity prices had risen two to threefold, while people had made sacrifices in the hope that economic conditions would improve. PTI leader and former KP finance minister Taimur Saleem Jhagra criticised government spending, questioning the reported purchase of a jet costing Rs10 billion and expenditure on official and private travel. He said every rupee of public money should be accounted for and questioned why relief was not being provided to people facing rising fuel prices. On Friday, days after the meeting reportedly took place, Naqvi declared that the government would stop anyone from marching towards the federal capital “in every possible way”. He further warned of contempt of court proceedings against those who violated the recent ruling by the Islamabad High Court (IHC), wherein it termed any activity resulting in infringement of citizens’ fundamental rights as a violation of the Constitution. “The question is not whether a political party is entitled to protest. It plainly is, subject always to the Constitution and law,” the judgment observed. KP CM meets Achakzai, Abbas Abbas’ remarks come after earlier in the day, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi met him and NA Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai to discuss the PTI’s upcoming protest. In a post on X, TTAP said the KP CM held an “important meeting” with Abbas and Achakzai, who is also the TTAP chairman. Yousafzai was also present on the occasion. “Detailed political consultations regarding the call for September 27 were held during the meeting, and various aspects of the future course of action, political strategy, and advancing the democratic struggle in an effective manner were discussed,” the statement said. The politicians consulted on taking forward the protest call as an “effective and organised political struggle for upholding the supremacy of the Constitution, democratic rights, provincial rights, and the protection of the public mandate”. The trio had also met on Thursday , shortly after CM Afridi concluded his visit to Punjab, where the upcoming protest was among the topics discussed. As part of the PTI’s preparations, the KP CM toured Sindh and Punjab to mobilise supporters for the protest. During his visit to the PML-N-led Punjab, Afridi not only alleged he was “ abducted ” by authorities in Lahore and later “thrown” by the roadside, but also claimed a man was sent to kill him. The Punjab government had swiftly refuted the claims of arrest, while the Wazirabad police clarified that the man accused by Afridi was a police constable deployed on security duty for the KP CM. The administrations of the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad had already begun preparations last week to counter the PTI’s announced march to the capital, including a request for the detention of activists, arranging containers, seeking additional personnel and procuring anti-riot gear.

Kohat Police Lines attack: 8 terrorists killed as overnight clearance operation concludes. PESHAWAR: Police said on Saturday that an overnight clearance operation following the deadly two-pronged assault near a mosque in Kohat district’s old Police Lines had been completed, saying that a total of eight terrorists were killed. After detonating an explosives-laden vehicle near a mosque in old Police Lines during Friday prayers, terrorists stormed the compound and attacked police facilities, martyring at least 21 and injuring over 100. The death toll rose to 23 on Saturday, including 17 policemen and six civilians, police and Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) officials confirmed. In an official handout, KP police said on Saturday that eight terrorists were killed in retaliatory action by police and security forces. It said that the operation had concluded, adding that Elite Force commandos, CTD teams, and security forces had cleared key parts of the buildings. According to the statement, KP Inspector General (IG) Zulfiqar Hameed was present at the scene. It added that the operation was led by the CTD additional IG, the Kohat regional police officer and the Kohat district police officer. It said that the Kohat general officer commanding was also present. “Law enforcement agencies achieved success following an overnight operation,” it said. The statement said IG Hameed commended the officers who participated in the operation and announced rewards for them. “Police, CTD, and security forces fought valiantly; these brave personnel are the pride of the nation,” he said. “The terrorists’ nefarious designs have been thwarted, and we will ensure their complete elimination,” he said. Army personnel stand amid the rubble following an explosion inside the police headquarters at Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on September 18, 2026. — AFP A CTD statement earlier said that its additional IG was injured in a grenade attack by terrorists during the operation. According to the statement, the terrorists had entered the Special Branch building after the suicide attack on the mosque. The statement said the CTD additional IG had been on the frontline since Friday afternoon, supervising the ongoing operation against Fitna al-Khawarij along with police personnel. The state uses the term Fitna al-Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). It said the additional IG sustained a hand injury in a grenade attack carried out by the terrorists during the operation. After receiving first aid, he returned to the frontline to supervise the operation and boost the morale of the personnel, the statement added. While the KP police stated the number of terrorists killed as eight, a statement by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi put it at seven. In the statement, Naqvi paid tribute to the security forces for eliminating “all seven” attackers. The interior minister said he was proud of all the brave personnel who participated in the operation. He added that the martyrs of the blast set the “highest example of duty by sacrificing their lives” and their sacrifices will be remembered. Relief efforts conclude Rescue 1122 also completed its relief and rescue operation on Saturday, with 24 vehicles — including ambulances, rescue vehicles and recovery vehicles — taking part in the efforts. In a statement, Rescue 1122 said Kohat District Emergency Officer Noorul Amin Khattak monitored the rescue operation, in which more than 60 personnel took part.
