Rescuers and vehicles from other districts, including Karak and Hangu, also assisted in the relief efforts. Seven of the injured were referred to Peshawar for further treatment, with five of them taken to Lady Reading Hospital and two to Hayatabad Medical Complex. Rescue 1122 spokesperson Bilal Ahmed Faizi noted that the personnel effectively conducted the relief and rescue efforts in “extremely tough, sensitive and dangerous conditions” while demonstrating excellent professional skills. ‘Pakistan has will, capability to protect its citizens’ The Ministry of Information strongly condemned the terrorist attack on civilians and police officials offering Friday prayers in Kohat, saying Pakistan had repeatedly raised concerns with the Afghan Taliban over the use of Afghan territory by terrorist groups to plan and carry out attacks inside the country. In a statement, the ministry said the presence of terrorist sanctuaries and recruitment and support networks in Afghanistan posed a direct threat to Pakistan’s security. It said these concerns had repeatedly been conveyed to the Afghan Taliban regime and its interlocutors, urging them to dismantle the networks instead of deflecting responsibility. The ministry also criticised Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid for threatening Pakistan with a “crushing response”, saying the Afghan Taliban should address the terrorist networks operating under their patronage. It said Pakistan had noted the Afghan Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ condemnation of the Kohat attack and expression of sympathy for the victims’ families, but regretted that the statement did not mention terrorism. The ministry said condemnation should be accompanied by “concrete action”, calling on the Afghan Taliban to take credible, verifiable and sustained measures to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries and disrupt recruitment and training networks. “Pakistan has both the will and the capability to eliminate terrorist threats wherever they are and will take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law, to protect its citizens, territory and sovereignty.” It added Pakistan remained committed to dialogue and constructive engagement but would take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law, to protect its citizens, territory and sovereignty, and urged the international community to press the Afghan Taliban to take action against terrorist groups. KP CM visits injured, bereaved families Separately, Chief Minister Sohail Afridi visited those injured in the blast and the families of those martyred, KP Information Minister Shafi Jan said. CM Afridi directed the relevant authorities to provide the wounded with the best possible medical facilities, and extended his condolences to the bereaved families. “He assured the affected families that the government stands with them and they will be provided with every possible support during this difficult time,” the statement said. CM Afridi had sought a detailed report on the incident on Friday, saying the targeting of innocent citizens was “deeply regrettable and unacceptable”. “The nation’s morale cannot be dampened by cowardly acts of terrorism,” he had said in a statement issued by his office following the blast. The attack was claimed by the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led Ittehadul Mujahideen. Funeral prayers for 15 of the martyred police personnel were offered in Kohat on Friday evening, after which their bodies were transported to their native districts of Kohat, Karak, Lakki Marwat, Bannu and Mardan in Rescue 1122 ambulances. Among the slain were SP Traffic Akbar Shinwari, head of the paediatric department at DHQ Hospital Dr Israel Orakzai, and Special Branch and CTD officials. It may be recalled that in 2010, 20 people, mostly relatives of policemen, were killed and more than 90 injured in a remote-controlled bomb blast inside a police colony located just behind the Kohat Police Lines. The explosion had taken place in Ramazan during Iftar.

Trump lists 25 'top achievements' as midterms loom. President Donald Trump claimed he halted all refugee admissions and made English the official language of the United States in a long list of what he called his top achievements, as difficult midterm elections loom. Trump is scrambling to boost his low approval ratings ahead of November’s vote, with polls showing the unpopular war in Iran and the fuel and other price rises it has caused are hurting his Republican Party. Polls say the party could well lose control of the House and perhaps even the Senate, a setback which would pose a major challenge for Trump and his America-first agenda in the last two years of his second term. Trump said Friday he “achieved the most secure border in history” in a lengthy social media post on Truth Social that focused on immigration, foreign policy and the economy. “ZERO illegal aliens admitted to the United States in the past 16 months,” he wrote, adding that his administration had slashed refugee admissions from “dangerous places”. Trump has presided over an often violent immigration crackdown which involves frequent deportations and shipping people whom the US cannot legally send home to third countries, which are sometimes compensated with money. He also claimed the US had “obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity” to ensure the Islamic republic “will NEVER have a nuclear weapon”. This was one of Trump’s often-changing justifications for going to war in February. The US-Israeli strikes on Tehran have rocked the global economy and engulfed the Middle East in war, proving a quagmire for a president who promised not to get America involved in any more foreign wars. Trump also flaunted hefty tariffs slapped on US trading partners, which he said were to “bring back American manufacturing”.

Govt, JI talks end inconclusively as Islamabad seeks delay in long march over security threats. LAHORE: The fifth round of talks between the government and the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) concluded on Saturday, with the government seeking the postponement of the party’s planned long march due to security threats. The government delegation included Federal Minister for Planning Ahsan Iqbal, Rana Sanaullah and Punjab Minister Khawaja Salman Rafique. The JI delegation comprised Deputy Emir Liaquat Baloch, Acting Secretary General Nazir Ahmad Janjua, Special Assistant to the JI Emir Umair Idrees, JI Lahore Emir Ziauddin Ansari and Information Secretary Shakeel Ahmad Tarrabi. During the talks, the government delegation requested the JI to postpone the long march in view of security threats. However, Baloch said the long march would remain necessary until the levy imposed on the public was withdrawn. The government levies Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. The JI has been staging regular sit-ins in Lahore, Peshawar, Karachi and dozens of other locations across the country since August 16 to protest the levy. The government delegation assured the JI that extraordinary relief would soon be provided to the people. It also said the government was under pressure from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and that an IMF delegation was expected to visit Pakistan shortly. Baloch said the government must take practical steps to address the people’s demands; otherwise, the JI would definitely proceed with its protest and long march. He said that, as per the schedule, the “ Super Long March ” under the leadership of the JI emir would begin from Karachi on Sunday. Talks between the JI and the government began on Sept 7 and have so far comprised four inconclusive rounds. The fifth round on Saturday also ended without an agreement. ‘No turning back’ Earlier, the party dug its heels in over its planned march, refusing to call it off unless the government abolishes the petroleum levy, with party chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman announcing that protest caravans from across the country would begin moving toward the capital on Sunday. “If the rulers cannot abolish the levy, we cannot call off our march,” Rehman said at a press conference in Mansoorah, setting the stage for a potential standoff with the authorities. The government, equipped with a recent Islamabad High Court (IHC) ruling against activities that curtail the freedom of movement, is determined to prevent rallies from disrupting traffic and the normal flow of life in the federal capital. Rehman promised peaceful protest and warned the government not to take any action against the protesters. “A public rally will be held in Karachi on Saturday night, before the caravans set out for Islamabad on September 20,” he said. The JI chief urged the government to present a concrete proposal for abolishing the petroleum levy, noting the party had already rejected the government’s fuel relief package as inadequate. Under the government’s current relief scheme , eligible motorcycles, rickshaws, Qingqi rickshaws and cars up to 800cc are to receive a subsidy of Rs100 per litre, subject to specified monthly limits. Rehman said relief was not a favour but a right of the people, accusing the government of avoiding structural measures to reduce the burden on consumers, saying petroleum prices had a direct impact on the cost of essential commodities across the country. He claimed that up to Rs107 per litre was being collected as petroleum levy on petrol, in addition to other taxes. The JI chief criticised the government for failing to curb corruption and what he described as “excessive official expenditure”, saying officials should reduce their own spending instead of asking the people to make sacrifices. To absorb the economic impact of renewed tensions in the Middle East, the government has reintroduced austerity measures, reducing fuel provision for official vehicles by 50 per cent for a period of three months. Islamabad march Rehman noted that the JI’s protest movement had entered its 35th day, with more than 25 sit-ins continuing across the country. He said the party had held peaceful demonstrations in 42 cities and claimed that the movement had now become a national issue. “We are marching for the people with their support. There is no question of turning back,” he said, insisting that the number of sit-ins was being gradually reduced as part of the JI’s strategy for the Islamabad march. The JI chief said the government had again contacted the party for talks, but repeatedly sought more time. “If the government does not listen to talks, it will have to listen to public pressure,” he said. On the PTI’s protest planned for September 27 for its incarcerated founder Imran Khan, Rehman said peaceful protest was a constitutional right of every political party and that containers should not be placed to block PTI demonstrations. He said the JI supported the PTI’s right to peaceful protest, while the PTI had also supported the JI’s right to do so. Economic policies criticised On negotiations , Rehman said the government had repeatedly asked the JI to submit suggestions, although, he argued, it was the government’s responsibility to address public grievances. He recalled that his party had already presented proposals during previous rounds of talks, but the government did not accept them. Rehman also criticised the government’s economic policies, calling for a reduction in interest rates and questioning the State Bank of Pakistan’s autonomy. He argued that the government’s role in appointments to the central bank raised questions about its independence. He further accused the government of using the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as an excuse for withholding relief from the public while continuing what he described as lavish official expenditure. Citing foreign travel by senior officials and expenses incurred at official meetings, the JI chief called on Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz to sell her official aircraft, which he valued at Rs11 billion. Turning to the sugar and wheat sectors, the party chief alleged that powerful groups and cartels were influencing government decisions on imports and exports, further alleging farmers were not receiving adequate prices for wheat and sugarcane, contributing to higher food prices. He also criticised payments to independent power producers (IPPs), saying Rs1.8 trillion was being paid in capacity payments. He further questioned payments to regasification plants despite what he described as gas shortages. JI Acting Secretary General Nazir Ahmad Janjua, Vice Emir Dr Usama Razi and Deputy Secretary Azhar Iqbal Hassan were also present at the press conference. On Friday, Rehman claimed the party’s protest movement aimed to press the government for immediate economic relief, asserting that the national exchequer could save between Rs3 trillion and Rs4 trillion if the authorities adopted the party’s proposed fiscal reforms.

DPM Dar to arrive ahead of PM Shehbaz’s UNGA visit, hold preliminary consultations. UNITED NATIONS: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar will arrive in New York on Sunday for preliminary consultations, a day before Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif arrives to lead the Pakistani delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Dar’s early arrival will allow Pakistan to prepare for a week of intensive diplomatic activity, as world leaders gather in New York amid the continuing war involving the United States, Israel and Iran, an escalating conflict in Yemen and growing tensions across the Middle East. The premier is due to arrive on Monday and will address the General Assembly on September 25. The Pakistani delegation has been significantly streamlined as part of the government’s austerity measures. Dar and senior foreign-policy adviser Tariq Fatemi will form the core of the prime minister’s delegation, while several federal ministers who had initially been expected to travel have been dropped from the trip, according to sources at the country’s UN mission. Information and Broadcasting Minister Attaullah Tarar, Minister for Climate Change and Environment Dr Musadik Malik and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal are among those not attending, added the sources. Dar’s preparatory meetings are expected to focus on Pakistan’s priorities for the UNGA high-level week and the rapidly changing regional situation. The Middle East crisis has already figured prominently in discussions at the UN headquarters, with the Security Council holding several meetings on the deteriorating situation in Yemen and the wider region in recent days. The General Assembly’s high-level general debate begins on Tuesday, when US President Donald Trump is scheduled to address the 81st session. The debate will run from Sept 22-26 and resume on Sept 28. US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said Trump was expected to highlight his administration’s handling of international crises and what it describes as its diplomatic achievements. “We expect the president will highlight how he and his administration have confronted complex problems head-on around the world,” Waltz said. He added Trump was also expected to stress “the importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon” and discuss progress on the administration’s 20-point Gaza peace plan. The General Assembly is convening as the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran continues to reverberate across the region. The crisis has been accompanied by heightened tensions in the Gulf, attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed threats to commercial shipping through the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. On Friday, the UN Security Council strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes affecting civilian and energy infrastructure that have caused civilian casualties, including women and children. The Council also condemned the Houthi military escalation in Yemen and attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb. The Council called for an immediate end to the Houthi military escalation and attacks affecting civilians and civilian objects. The statement came as Saudi Arabia faced another wave of Houthi attacks. The escalation in Yemen is likely to figure among the issues discussed by Pakistani officials during UNGA week. Pakistan has already condemned Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and commercial shipping and reaffirmed its support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Pakistan’s UN ambassador, Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, has also called for restraint and peaceful resolution of regional disputes. For Islamabad, the Middle East crisis presents a sensitive diplomatic challenge. Pakistan maintains close relations with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states while also sharing a border and longstanding ties with Iran. Against this backdrop, Pakistan is expected to emphasise diplomacy, dialogue and peaceful resolution of conflicts, while raising the Palestinian issue and the Kashmir dispute at the General Assembly. PM Shehbaz’s agenda will also include sustainable development, climate action, counterterrorism, Islamophobia and reform of the United Nations. He is expected to hold bilateral meetings with world leaders and the UN secretary-general. For Pakistan, the immediate task will be to advance its diplomatic priorities while responding to a rapidly changing security environment in a region of direct strategic importance to Islamabad.

Denmark hails 'binding' Greenland deal with Trump. Denmark on Saturday hailed a “binding” deal announced by US President Donald Trump to give Washington “permanent control“ over Greenland’s security and bar Russian and Chinese bases from the Arctic territory. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance. Denmark and Greenland — an autonomous Danish territory — both hailed the agreement and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week. “A long period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a social media post on Saturday. The deal respected Denmark’s “red lines” and was “important” in light of a changed security situation, he said. ‘Permanent control’ While the terms are still unclear, Denmark maintains that its sovereignty remains intact. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement with Washington “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. It was “good for NATO and Europe”, she said. Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal “recognises Greenland’s interests” and “strengthens” its security. In Greenland’s capital Nuuk, residents had mixed feelings. “I don’t know exactly what the agreement is or what has been signed. But whenever the US and Trump are mentioned, I have mixed feelings. I’m not entirely comfortable with how much attention Greenland has right now,” Soren Kreutzmann, a 29-year-old hairdresser, told AFP. “We hope the leaders have made a good agreement, because our country needs to be protected, both from the air and sea. Denmark had not given that enough attention for many years,” said Bibbi Kleist Jepsen, a 64-year-old pedagogue. Trump hailed the deal as an “ ’Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!”. Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory, he added. “From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.” While Trump presented the deal as a major triumph, Danish commentators said he had likely gained little. They noted that, under a 1951 defence pact updated in 2004, Washington was already able to ramp up its military presence on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance. “Shhh. Don’t tell Trump that it’s the Kingdom of Denmark that has prevailed,” US correspondent Jacob Heinel Jensen wrote in Danish newspaper Berlingske on Saturday. Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, said Trump “obviously didn’t get in this agreement what he originally set out to have, that is, sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States”. China, Russia concerns Trump has repeatedly warned of Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle unfolds for supremacy in a warming Arctic. The State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so. “This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” a State Department official said. Gad noted that while Russia had little interest in Greenland, China was investing in extractive industries to get a foothold in the Arctic. “The US is worried that any kind of Chinese footprint could be turned into military assets,” he said. Cautioning that the details of the deal remained unknown, Gad said “the worrisome thing here is this exclusive access for the US to build bases in Greenland and how that involves NATO allies from Europe. “Trump has been flirting with breaking up the NATO alliance… If Europe is an adversary, how would that position Europe, Denmark and Greenland in that situation?” Furthermore, “if the US can also veto European investments in Greenland, that would be highly controversial.” Several media outlets have reported that Washington wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory. At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO. Tensions have since eased. In an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Houthis say targeted 'sensitive sites' in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Yemen’s Houthis said on Saturday that they launched strikes targeting “sensitive sites” in Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and oil facilities in the kingdom’s port city of Yanbu, hours after residents reported blasts in the Saudi capital. This is the first time since Yemen’s long-standing civil war resumed that it has threatened the Saudi capital, further shaking a global economy already under pressure by nearly seven months of war between the United States and Iran. “In response to the Saudi enemy’s attempts to target the capital Sana’a… the Yemeni Armed Forces carried out two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, in a statement on Telegram. “The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu.” This photo shows a general view of fuel tanks at the fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on September 19, 2026. —AFP The Houthi statement came after firefighters extinguished a blaze on a fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil giant Aramco at a fuel depot near Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday, according to an AFP journalist. Smoke plume near Riyadh airport A large plume of smoke was visible near Riyadh’s main airport after booms were heard and Saudi Arabia sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around the capital, amid an escalation in attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. Reuters video and photographs showed a huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. Aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24 reported major issues at the Saudi capital’s Riyadh King Khalid International Airport, including cancellations and delays. The airport was listed under the site’s maximum disruption index of 5.0, meaning the airport was seeing “major problems with long delays and several cancelled flights”. There was no immediate comment from the Saudi government’s media office in response to Reuters’ questions about the smoke and the overnight alerts. Saudi civil defence sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential danger in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. “The area is under a hostile aerial threat,” said a message received just before 3:00am by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors. AFP journalists then heard two explosions, before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later. A Reuters journalist in Riyadh’s Olaya area also heard booms before the all-clear was sent. “I heard the alarm, then my windows shook,” a Riyadh resident, 27, living in the city’s north, told AFP . “It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this.” Another resident described the attack as “terrifying”. “I was extremely anxious — especially because, unlike previous times, the ‘all-clear’ signal didn’t come right away,” the central Riyadh resident said. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the threat mentioned in the warnings sent overnight to residents of several regions and has not identified where it originated from. Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation began with the Houthis in July. The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Makkah on Wednesday, denouncing it as a “cowardly terrorist attack” on the holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year. Houthis strongly denied the accusation , calling it a “worn-out lie”. Houthi attacks The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks towards Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea. The attacks have created new threats to global oil supplies, putting at risk trade via Bab al-Mandab — the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports — while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains blockaded. The Houthis insist there is no threat to shipping in the sea lane — except for Saudi ships, from the world’s leading crude exporter. On Friday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group, which seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning advance this month, says the Saudi Air Force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days. The UN Security Council (UNSC) in a statement on Friday “condemned in the strongest terms continued Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children”. In the statement, the UNSC also condemned “Houthi military escalation in Yemen”. The US, according to Axios , last week refused to strike the Houthis at Saudi Arabia’s request. On Thursday, Washington approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom to help Riyadh “deter current and future threats”, the US State Department said. The attack targeting Riyadh comes as the Houthis improve their defences in newly conquered territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels. The United Nations said on Friday that the renewed fighting had displaced more than 112,000 people while nearly 3,000 others had fled across the sea to Djibouti. The war in Yemen broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015. The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July , when the Houthis defied Riyadh’s control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.

‘GB peaks more valuable than oil reservoirs’. Reinhold Messner and his wife, Diane, climb a rock to view Nanga Parbat, remembering when he and his late brother, Gunther, climbed that same rock in 1970 before their historic expedition.—Photo by the writer • Renowned climber Messner warns ‘white mountains’ may not survive another decade; calls for urgent action • Celebrates 82nd birthday in Islamabad • Reflects on his lifelong bond with Pakistan ISLAMABAD: Renowned Italian mountaineer Reinhold Messner warned that rapid glacial melting threatens the survival of Pakistan’s peaks, declaring the high mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan “more valuable than oil reservoirs in Arab countries”. Expressing deep concern for the changing environment, the alpinist said some “white mountains” in the region may only survive another 10 to 15 years without better environmental management, pledging that he and his team remain determined to help save the remaining ice. The 82-year-old issued the warning while celebrating his birthday during a 12-day visit to the mountain areas of GB with his wife, Diane. The trip, which ran from Sept 6 to Sept 16, culminated in a birthday celebration organised by Nanga Parbat Adventure Pakistan at the Serena Hotel in Islamabad. Italian Ambassador to Pak­istan Ugo Ciarlatani, German Ambassador Ina Lepel and prominent Pakistani mountaineers, including Nazir Sabir and Liver Khan, attended the ceremony to honour Messner’s historic achievements. Beyond his climbing legacy, Mr Messner continues to give back to the region. Mr Khan, a long-time friend, highlighted Messner’s ongoing connection to the local communities that aided him during his perilous descent of Nanga Parbat over 50 years ago. Over the decades, Mr Messner has helped establish several schools in the Diamer valleys, including one named in memory of his younger brother, Mr Gunther. “I look forward to … the schools, places where the future is written, where hope grows stronger than loss,” Mr Messner noted. The return to Pakistan brought profound sentimental reflections for the man widely regarded as one of history’s greatest high-altitude climbers. Days before his birthday, Mr Messner stopped at a rock situated along the Karakoram Highway near Thalichy, which offers a clear view of Nanga Parbat. He climbed the rock again, just as he did in 1970 when he and Mr Gunther first saw the mountain rising in the distance. For Mr Messner, the region holds both triumph and deep personal tragedy. He and Mr Gunther reached the summit of Nanga Parbat in 1970 via the Rupal Face, but disaster struck during their descent on the Diamir side. Mr Gunther was swept away by an avalanche and died. Mr Messner survived but lost seven toes to severe frostbite. His cla­ims about his brother’s death were vindicated in 2005 when Mr Gunther’s remains were fin­ally discovered on the Diamir Face. Mr Messner was accused by his teammates, including Herrl­igko­ffer, of abandoning his bro­ther solely to gain the bragging rights of traversing Nanga Parbat. In 1978, Mr Messner returned to summit Nanga Parbat completely alone. Climbing without supplementary oxygen or support from teammates, he opened a new route on the right side of the Diamir Face, completing the first solo ascent of an 8,000-metre mountain. “To return to Pakistan is to return to the roots of my own becoming,” Mr Messner wrote in a social media post before his arrival. “Here, at Nanga Parbat, I crossed the mountain and lost my brother Gunther, a wound that has never closed but became part of who I am.” Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

Govt finalises sweeping civil service reforms. • 11 specialised professional cadres in bureaucracy proposed • BS-20, above posts may be opened to officials, academics, private-sector professionals ISLAMABAD: Amid concerns over declining standards and lack of specialisation in the bureaucracy, the federal government has finalised a sweeping restructuring of the civil service, proposing 11 new professional cadres, a complete overhaul of the Central Superior Services (CSS) examination and senior-level promotions and linking officials’ performance to financial rewards. The proposed reforms, estimated to cost Rs11 billion to implement, seek to reshape recruitment, training, career progression, performance evaluation and the institutional structure of the federal bureaucracy. The package was unveiled at a consultative session on civil service reforms chaired by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal on Saturday. The session was attended by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, Federal Minister Aleem Khan, former PTI federal minister Asad Umar, senior policymakers, sector specialists and other stakeholders. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had constituted two committees on civil service reforms, which have held 18 meetings since September 2024 and reached consensus on 43 of 46 recommendations. The proposed new professional cadres include HR, Law, Engine­ering, Science and Technology, IT and Telecom, Energy, Climate, Agriculture and Forestry, Education and Health groups. The Establishment Division wou­ld be converted into a Human Reso­urce and Organisation Development Division, while federal decision-making would be reduced from five tiers to three. Under the proposed National Executive Service (NES) structure, posts in BS-20 and above would be filled through open competition on five-year contracts against published performance targets, with serving officers, private-sector professionals and academics competing on equal terms. The Police Service and Foreign Service would remain outside the NES. It also proposes piloting performance-linked pay in the federal secretariat and a retirement package comprising a Rs5 million lump sum funded through monthly deductions, along with subsidised health insurance. The new policy also draws on Pakistan Army human resource practices, proposing replacement of the one-day viva voce with a multi-day competency-based assessment on the pattern of ISSB. The model emphasises psychometric, emotional intelligence and leadership assessments at recruitment, placement on the principle of the “right person for the right job”, specialised training and multi-tier performance evaluation. It also draws on the army’s structured promotion system, under which progression becomes increasingly selective at senior ranks and promotion decisions are made collectively by boards on prescribed criteria rather than individual discretion. A key shift under the proposed system is recruitment according to specialisation, ending the existing arrangement under which officers can be allocated to fields they have never studied. The CSS examination itself would not be abolished. Candidates would have the option of attempting five compulsory papers — Essay, Précis and Composition, Islamiat, Pakistan Studies and Current Affairs — in Urdu, while functional proficiency in English would remain a screening requirement. The preliminary test threshold would be raised from 33pc to 40pc, with analytical reasoning added and negative marking removed. The package also proposes published assessment criteria, full digitisation and reduction of the recruitment cycle to six months or less, alongside affirmative measures to fill unfilled quota seats for Balochistan, Sindh, minorities and women. The performance system would also be recast, with every ministry entering into an annual performance agreement with the prime minister and individual targets flowing from it. Officials would be evaluated twice a year, while 5pc of employee-related expenditure would be earmarked for performance-based honoraria. The National Management Course would be shortened from 18 weeks to 10, while existing national and specialised training institutions would be merged into a National University of Public Administration. No constitutional amendment would be required for the package. Following approval, an implementation committee would oversee execution, report monthly to the prime minister and target full implementation within 120 days. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

SMOKERS’ CORNER: WHY THE PPP DOMINATES SINDH. Despite persistent criticism in the mainstream media, the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) maintains an almost invincible electoral grip on Sindh. Standing against this dominance is a fragile opposition, historically anchored by the Pakistan Muslim League-Functional (PML-F) and currently consolidated under the banner of the Grand Democratic Alliance (GDA). Such opposition coalitions in Sindh often assemble around the PML-F and an eclectic mix of disgruntled former PPP members, local Sindhi nationalist groups, the Mohajir/Urdu-speaking nationalist party the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM), and federal players such as the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI). The alliances have consistently failed to curb the PPP’s dominance in the province. Deconstructing this failure requires revisiting the origins of the PML-F itself. The party’s roots trace back to the mid-1950s, when Pakistan’s founding party, the Muslim League, fragmented into various self-serving factions. By the early 1960s, three primary streams dominated the League’s fractured existence: the Convention Muslim League (formed in 1962 under military dictator Gen Ayub Khan), the Council Muslim League (organised the same year by League veterans discarded by Gen Ayub) and the East Pakistan-centred Awami League. Ahead of the 1965 presidential election, the Council League partnered with an array of leftist and Islamist parties to form the anti-Ayub Combined Opposition Parties (COP) alliance. Following COP’s defeat, its presidential candidate, Fatima Jinnah, spearheaded the creation of a distinct Muslim League faction, appointing the influential Sindhi politician and spiritual leader Pir Pagara to its central leadership, a move that birthed the PML-F. Sindh’s ruling party’s electoral dominance in the province rests on more than patronage networks. The inability of opposition parties such as the PML-F to challenge PPP’s hold over Sindhi identity and economic realities and to build grassroots organisations have played as much of a role During the PPP’s first government in the centre (1971-77), the PML-F was part of the parliamentary opposition. Pagara viewed the PPP chairman and fellow Sindhi Z.A. Bhutto as an upstart. Due to his spiritual status, Pagara saw himself as the true heir to Sindh’s politics and positioned his party as an extension of the country’s founding party. In late 1976, Pagara joined the anti-PPP coalition, the Pakistan National Alliance (PNA), to contest the 1977 parliamentary election. He was also at the forefront of the violent PNA movement against the Bhutto regime, after the alliance accused the government of rigging the elections. In July 1977, when Gen Ziaul Haq toppled the government, Pagara moved close to the military regime. Illustration by Abro After the Zia dictatorship executed Bhutto in 1979 through a controversial trial, Pagara began to shape the PML-F as Sindh’s leading political force. With the dictatorship’s backing, he reorganised the PML-F, not as a mass-based party, but as a conservative, pro-establishment counterweight to the left-leaning, anti-establishment wave that swept Sindh in the wake of Bhutto’s execution. By establishing itself as an entity tied closely to state patronage and a military-backed government, the PML-F traded long-term grassroots political organisation for short-term institutional influence. The party’s voting base remained limited to the allegiance of Pagara’s spiritual followers, restricting its electoral viability within specific, geographical pockets of the province. After Zia’s demise in 1988, subsequent generations of PMLF-led anti-PPP coalitions in Sindh adopted this same structure. Rather than building institutional party branches, cultivating a compelling platform or mobilising the public around economic issues, the opposition in the province continued to function as a loose conglomerate of localised feudal fiefdoms operating under the leadership of Pagara, and later under his son, Syed Sibghatullah Shah Rashdi III. The failure of these opposition alliances stems primarily from the PPP’s mastery over the provincial patronage network that it weaved and its control over the narrative of Sindhi identity. Since 2008, the PPP has astutely utilised the provincial machinery as a widespread influence mechanism. Through the control of provincial institutions and social safety nets, such as the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP), the PPP commands the material reality of life in Sindh’s regions where Sindhi-speakers are in the majority. This strategy has left the PML-F and other anti-PPP parties in Sindhi-majority areas restricted to tiny pockets. Landed elites in the PML-F and GDA struggle to compete with a centralised PPP-led provincial government that holds the strings of public resources. The PPP has successfully presented itself as the sole defender of Sindh’s economic and cultural rights. Even when the PPP had a huge vote bank in Punjab (1970–2008), the party’s Sindh chapters were actively evolving this narrative. The roots of this narrative can be found in Bhutto’s two-pronged strategy in the 1970s. While the party’s overall disposition was federal (and still is), in Sindh, Bhutto usurped the Sindhi nationalist narrative that was first shaped by the likes of G.M. Syed and Sheikh Ayaz. The PPP then diluted it and placed the narrative firmly within a federal context. The PML-F lacks the intellectual rigour to replicate anything of the sort and constantly seeks support from powerful state institutions, such as the military establishment. Whenever the PML-F or the GDA enters into tactical electoral alliances with federal parties, such as the PML-N or PTI, or urban Mohajir-centric outfits such as the MQM, most Sindhis view this as an attempt to mitigate Sindh’s provincial autonomy. In this case, even though most Sindhi nationalist groups are part of GDA, they often choose not to partner with the PML-F. This dynamic becomes even more intricate when examining the politics of anti-PPP Sindhis residing in Sindh’s cosmopolitan capital Karachi. The city’s upper-middle and middle class Sindhis are often critics of the PPP. Yet, this demographic exhibits a pragmatic outlook. Within the socio-political spaces of Karachi, where their language and cultural heritage have historically been sidelined by urban power structures, Karachi’s Sindhis experience an acute sense of minority status. Their response to this environment is a protective reliance on the very party they criticise in private. For Karachi’s middle class Sindhis, the PPP serves a dual function. It regulates the dominance of non-Sindhi political forces and prevents the administrative division of Karachi. Economically, the city’s Sindhis rely heavily on the provincial state apparatus to secure their socio-economic standing in a private sector that is otherwise dominated by non-Sindhi business communities. For Karachi-based Sindhis, challenging the PPP’s dominance risks undermining the single political institution that guarantees their economic and political inclusion. Anti-PPP Sindhis spread across Karachi view the alternative represented by the PML-F as either completely aligned with federal forces or entirely incapable of protecting Sindhi interests in the metropolis. The anti-PPP opposition in Sindh remains trapped in a cycle. By relying on legacy spiritual authority, localised feudal figures and state patronage rather than building an inclusive, progressive and organised political alternative, parties such as the PML-F have miserably failed to challenge the PPP in any meaningful manner. As long as the opposition fails to address the deep-seated ethnic, economic and existential anxieties of Sindhis, the electoral dominance of the PPP in Sindh will endure. Published in Dawn, EOS, September 20th, 2026

Power consumers may face Rs1.73/unit tariff hike. ISLAMABAD: Elec­tri­city consumers across the country may face a Rs1.73 per unit increase following a request to adjust power tariffs under the monthly fuel adjustment mechanism for August. The Central Power Purchasing Agency (CPPA) has filed the application with the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra), which will hear the request on Sept 29. The proposed increase will also apply to consumers of K-Electric (KE), according to the request. The CPPA said 14.464 billion units of electricity were supplied to distribution companies (Discos) in August at an average cost of Rs8.82 per unit. Generation mix Hydropower accounted for 37.84 per cent of total electricity generation during the month, while 10.88pc was generated from local coal and 15.59pc from imported coal. Electricity generated from furnace oil accounted for 2.15pc, while local gas contributed 7.04pc and imported LNG 8.48pc. The CPPA said the cost of electricity generated from furnace oil stood at Rs45.25 per unit, while power generated from imported LNG cost Rs45.92 per unit. Last month, Nepra approved an financial burden of about Rs9.8bn on electricity consumers by allowing a fuel cost adjustment of 75.03 paise per unit in August electricity bills. Nepra said it had decided that the positive FCA for June 2026, amounting to Rs0.7503 per kilowatt-hour, would be applicable to all consumer categories of KE and ex-Wapda distribution companies, except lifeline consumers, electric vehicle charging stations and pre-paid electricity consumers of all categories who had opted for the pre-paid tariff. The regulator had said the higher FCA would also apply to consumers under the incremental consumption package. Distribution companies and KE were directed to reflect the fuel cost adjustment for June this year in electricity bills issued for August. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

Security forces kill 5 terrorists, recover 23 abductees in operation along N-25 highway near Balochistan's Kalat: ISPR. Security forces have killed five terrorists and recovered 23 kidnapped individuals from their hideout during an operation along the N-25 Karachi-Chaman highway near Balochistan’s Kalat, the military’s media affairs wing said on Sunday. In a statement, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said that terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan tried to disrupt people’s movement by establishing a checkpost for abduction for ransom, extortion and snatching of vehicles along the N-25 highway, also knows as the Pakistan Expressway, on the night between Sept 18 and Sept 19. “Security forces responded immediately and after intense fire exchange, five terrorists belonging to India-sponsored proxy of Fitna-al-Hindustan were sent to hell,” the statement said. The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. According to the ISPR, 23 abductees were recovered from the terrorists’ hideout near Kalat. Six trucks, three buses and two cars were also recovered, as well as large quantities of weapons, ammunition and explosives, the statement said. “Successful operations by the security forces resulted in thwarting the nefarious designs of India-sponsored proxy of Fitna-al-Hindustan ,” it added. The ISPR said sanitisation operations were ongoing in the surrounding areas to eliminate any remaining terrorists and ensure the safety and security of the local population and national highways. “The relentless counter-terrorism campaign under the vision of ‘ Azm-i-Istehkam ’, as approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, will continue with full resolve. Security forces and law enforcement agencies remain committed to eliminating the menace of foreign-sponsored and foreign-supported terrorism from the country,” the statement concluded. Balochistan has been facing security challenges and terrorism, which has prompted security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to a monthly assessment by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. The ISPR and the state media has reported several actions in the province over recent weeks. On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, terrorists of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in the Pishin district. In retaliatory action, security forces killed 10 terrorists while two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, the military’s media affairs wing said. Also on August 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were killed following an intense exchange of fire. On September 2, security forces killed 12 terrorists in the Kalat district during an intelligence-based operation (IBO). Days later, the troops killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives during separate IBOs in Kharan and Washuk districts. Another 36 terrorists were eliminated during multiple “high-tempo” operations conducted in Mastung, Quetta, Kalat and Sibi districts, the Inter-Services Public Relations said on September 4. These also included thwarting an attack on a police station in Sibi’s Bhag area. On Thursday, seven terrorists were killed by security forces in an IBO in the Badrang area of Balochistan’s Awaran district, while seven terrorists were killed during two IBOs in the province’s Panjgur and Kachhi districts on Friday, the state media reported. The killing of 11 more terrorists by security forces in Panjgur and Chagai districts under Operation Raddul Fitna 3 was reported on Saturday.

Pakistan snubs Taliban’s ‘pretence of dialogue’. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan on Saturday said it had consistently pursued dialogue and constructive engagement with the Afghan Taliban, but would not allow what it called the “pretence of dialogue” to shield those threatening its people. The information ministry was responding to Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid’s remarks in an interview with Al Arabiya English a day earlier, in which he said Afghanistan wanted dialogue with Pakistan and called for stronger mechanisms for intelligence-sharing and cooperation. He also welcomed a larger Saudi role in mediating between Kabul and Islamabad, saying Saudi Arabia was a friend of both countries and could play a “positive role” in resolving their differences. Pakistan also rejected Kabul’s warning of “retaliatory action” if Islamabad carried out military operations inside Afghanistan, saying the Taliban regime should dismantle terrorist networks operating from its territory instead of “deflecting responsibility”. During the interview, Mr Mujahid warned Pakistan against conducting military operations inside Afghanistan and said Kabul would defend its sovereignty against any such action. Responding to Kabul spox seeking talks, Islamabad says Afghan govt should dismantle terrorists operating from its territory He also denied Islamabad’s assertion that Afghan territory was being used by militant groups to launch attacks inside Pakistan. “If Pakistan invokes Article 51 to violate the sanctity of Afghan territory, Afghanistan has the right to defend its country, and we will do so,” he said, warning of a “crushing response” to any violation of Afghan sovereignty. Pakistan reiterated that it had the “will and capability” to eliminate terrorist threats and would take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law, to protect its citizens, territory and sovereignty. Pakistan also linked the Afghan Taliban’s warning to the deadly terrorist attack on civilians and police officials offering Friday prayers in Kohat. “We strongly condemn the barbaric terrorist attack on civilians and police officials offering Friday prayers in Kohat,” the ministry of information stated, describing the attackers as “the vilest of Khwarij with roots in Afghanistan”. It said Pakistan had repeatedly raised concerns over the use of Afghan territory by Fitna al-Khawarij and other terrorist groups to plan and launch attacks inside Pakistan. The state uses the term Fitna al-Khawari j for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). “The presence of terrorist sanctuaries, alongside their recruitment and support infrastructure in Afghanistan, poses a direct threat to Pakistan’s security,” it said, adding that the concerns had repeatedly been conveyed to the Afghan Taliban regime and its interlocutors. The ministry said the Taliban must dismantle the networks instead of “deflecting responsibility”. Pakistan also rejected Mujahid’s assertion that Kabul did not allow the TTP to operate from Afghan territory or support armed groups targeting other countries. Pakistan said the Afghan Taliban had obligations under the Doha Agreement to prevent Afghan territory from being used to threaten other countries. It said it had noted the Afghan Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ condemnation of the Kohat attack and expression of sympathy for the victims’ families, but regretted that the statement did not mention terrorism. “Condemnation must be matched by concrete action,” the ministry said, calling on the Taliban to take “credible, verifiable and sustained measures” to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries and disrupt recruitment and training networks. Fuel relief scheme revised; SMS charges scrapped. ISLAMABAD: The government on Sa­­turday announced major chan­ges to the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Sche­­me , including abolition of SMS charges, to facilitate beneficiaries, particularly motorcycle, rickshaw and Qingqi users. Addressing a media briefing, Mi­nister for IT and Telecom­munication Shaza Fatima Khawaja said the Rs500 per-token limit for two- and three-wheelers had been abolished. Also, she said, eligible two- and three-wheeler users could obtain four tokens per month, with each token carrying a relief amount of Rs500. For example, if two litres of petrol cost Rs780, the beneficiary would pay Rs280 after applying the Rs500 relief token, she explained. She said another major change was the abolition of SMS charges across the board under the scheme. SMS had been made free for everyone, whether they owned an 800cc vehicle or a two- or three-wheeler, she said. Five-litre limit per token abolished; two- and three-wheeler users allowed four Rs500 relief tokens a month According to her, more than 1.75 million registrations had been completed under the scheme by 3pm on Saturday, while around 1.5m tokens had been generated. Redemption of fuel tokens Meanwhile, the National Stee­r­ing Committee on Fuel Subsidy, led by Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, approved redemption of fuel tokens through SMS for stations located in areas without internet connectivity. It asked Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan and the provinces to furnish lists of such stations so that they could be brought onto the scheme without delay. Registration continues nationwide through SMS to 9771. The meeting was attended by the ministers for petroleum, economic affairs, information and IT & telecommunications; SBP deputy governor, Ogra chairman; Pakistan Digital Authority chairman; petroleum secretary; ICT chief commissioner; additional chief secretaries of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtun­khwa; and senior officials from AJK, GB and Balochistan. Kohat attack. FRIDAY’S attack in Kohat marks a further escalation by Pakistan’s enemies. They targeted a mosque in Kohat’s old Police Lines with an explosives-laden vehicle, then attempted to storm the compound and attack police facilities in the ensuing chaos. At least 23, including 17 police personnel and officials, were martyred in this dastardly assault on worshippers. More than 100 were wounded. But police and security forces regrouped quickly and launched a valiant counterassault, eliminating all but two of the attackers within hours of the initial bombing. The remaining two were neutralised in a clean-up operation that extended overnight, supervised by some of the top police and counterterrorism officials, with one holed-up terrorist killed and the other blowing themselves up rather than face the consequences of their actions. The operation produced considerable acts of courage, not least by the additional inspector-general of the CTD, who was injured by a grenade yet returned to conclude the clean-up. The nation will mourn the lives lost and pray for those who were injured. The nation will also demand swift justice for those who lost loved ones. The group which claimed the attack has, by attacking worshippers on what Muslims consider the holiest occasion of the week, not only shown that it observes no ethical limits, but also that it is operating with a single goal: to cause maximum bloodshed and harm. The Ittehadul Mujahideen, an umbrella organisation of terrorist outfits, is, according to the Jamestown Foundation think tank, believed to operate from safe havens across the border, share intelligence and coordinate attacks with its terrorist factions, and run organised digital campaigns. It has apparently used drone technologies to deadly effect while targeting security forces and installations in the past. As such, it is considered in some circles to be a more serious and sophisticated threat than the TTP. It needs to be treated as such. The KP police must be better equipped and trained. They are facing an enemy which is increasingly using modern technology to cause bloodshed. They must be supported with the equipment, strategies and technologies they need to effectively limit and counter the constant, deadly threat they face. Simultaneously, the authorities need to review the approaches being taken to counter violent actors. National policy on counterterrorism requires recalibration and revisiting, especially regarding its diplomatic, political and social aspects, which must be addressed together to secure stable dividends. Sadly, the public’s attention is so fixated on social, political and economic problems that the terrorism crisis has been pushed to the margins of national discourse. Pakistan must confront these networks with the full force of the state and the law, but cannot do so effectively till its own house is in order. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

An eye on Balochistan border. THE intensifying Yemeni Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have triggered a debate over the possible activation of the Makkah accord . Statements and clarifications about possible and emerging scenarios are coming from all stakeholders. But a recent incident in Saravan county in Sistan-Baluchestan, close to the Pakistan border, has also drawn attention to the Iran-Pakistan border region. This has broadened the debate over the Gulf region’s security and evolving geopolitics, and Pakistan’s role in it. The incident was reported on Sept 12, when heavy fighting between Iranian security forces and unidentified gunmen spread across parts of Saravan, with reports of attacks on military vehicles and dozens of security personnel killed or wounded. Although the identity of the armed group is not yet clear, some analysts have attributed the attack to Jaish al-Adl or the People’s Fighters Front, an alliance of several groups, reportedly including Jaish al-Adl. Since the start of the conflict in West Asia, Balochistan’s security dynamics have changed. The conflict has altered the operating environment in which an existing insurgency was already functioning. The BLA and other allied groups have intensified their terrorist activities . The economic blockade announced by these groups has disrupted transportation and halted economic activity, particularly in the mineral sector. The closure of the frontier with Afghanistan and the partial closure of the border with Iran have contributed to the crisis. Taken together, these developments have affected the region’s security, internal political dynamics and geopolitical environment, bringing new risks to the province. An angle that has largely been overlooked in the broader conflict theatre in this area is the state of affairs along the Pakistan-Iran border, which stretches for around 900 kilometres and where multiple violent religious and nationalist insurgent groups, as well as transnational criminal networks, operate. The border’s porous nature raises further security concerns. According to media reports, Pakistani security institutions had placed Balochistan on high alert because of the possible fallout from the Iran war. The situation along the Pakistan-Iran border in the broader conflict has been largely overlooked. The Jan 16, 2024, Iranian strike inside Pakistan , allegedly targeting Jaish al-Adl hideouts, followed by Pakistan’s retaliatory strikes on militant targets in Iran, changed the dynamics of their bilateral relations and prompted greater security cooperation. That cooperation has largely remained intact. However, the recent Saravan attack has raised questions about how the changing regional environment could affect the future course of frontier security, particularly as Pakistan’s border with Afghanistan remains closed and Iran is an alternative, although very expensive, route for transnational trade. For Iran, if the Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) has to concentrate its resources on US and Israeli strikes, the Strait of Hormuz and operations in the Gulf, Sistan-Baluchestan could become a per­ipheral theatre competing for Iranian security resources. Any escalation of tensions betw­een Iran and Pakistan is in neither country’s interest. However, non-state actors always try to find an opportunity in evolving conflicts, especially when wider regional contexts provide them with more meaning and relevance in the conflict theatre. The BLA and other insurgent groups appear to have viewed the war as an opportunity to escalate their operations, perhaps hoping that they could eventually be considered as potential proxies against Iran, as happened in Syria with America’s partnership with the Syrian Demo­cratic Forces. The SDF was a coalition that included Kurdish armed groups such as the YPG and YPJ, along with Syrian Arab and Assyrian/ Christian elements. The BLA has also issued a few statements supporting US strikes on Iran. Perhaps the BLA believes it can find meaning in the wider conflict in West Asia. Still, the BLA is missing a point in its calculation: the convergence of US, Pakistani, and Saudi geopolitical and strategic interests will persist in the coming years. At the same time, Jaish al-Adl and several smaller groups have reportedly sought to broaden their activities against the Quds Force and IRGC. The group remained relatively quiet until Iranian security forces launched an operation against suspected terrorists in Saravan last August, reportedly apprehending several Jaish al-Adl members and killing one. During the operation, security forces said they recovered a significant arsenal of military hardware, including dozens of Kalash­nikov automatic rifles, hand grenades, RPG-7 launchers, around 20 kilograms of C-4 military-grade explosives, 150 rounds of ammunition, and several Starlink satellite internet devices. The Saravan operation reported last week has since been interpreted in multiple ways, mostly based on assumptions rather than established evidence. One popular theory links the attack to the intensification of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia. The incident also occurred while Pakistan was diplomatically engaged with Iran. According to a media report, subsequently denied by Pakistan, Islamabad had conveyed a Saudi message to Tehran asking Iran to restrain the Houthis. A popular perception in the border region of Balochistan is that if Iran can use the Houthis as a proxy against Saudi Arabia, it must also expect the possibility of a similar reaction from Saudi Arabia. The Sunni militias operating in Sistan-Baluchestan, from Jundullah to the People’s Fighters Front, are said to be proxies of foreign powers including the US and Saudi Arabia. That perception is nurturing new theories. A few of them are critical of Pakistan too. Whether such perceptions translate into an actual Saudi strategy is another question. But perceptions themselves can influence the behaviour of armed groups and local actors, particularly in a region where terrorist networks, cross-border tribal connections and informal economic networks overlap. Beyond all the theories surrounding the strategic calculus of West Asia and the prospects of Saudi proxies emerging along the Pakistan-Iran border, one fact remains clear: Pakistan cannot afford further chaos in the border region of Balochistan. Any expansion of the regional conflict in an already fragile security environment could make the country’s internal security dynamics considerably more complex. The writer is a security analyst. A small republic in every classroom. PAKISTAN is extraordinarily young. Two in every three of its people are under 30. The question is not whether Generation Z will change Pakistan. Demographically, it will. The question is whether it will be ready, and little in the way this country is arranged suggests it will. Their task can be stated in a sentence. The Constitution of Pakistan on paper and the Constitution as it works on the ground are two different documents, and the distance between them is what this generation has to close. I was 14 when martial law came and a young man when that general died. My generation learnt a dangerous lesson: power does not explain itself. The man who speaks out is transferred; the man who stays quiet is promoted; the judge who insists upon his independence is superseded. Caution, practised long enough, becomes accommodation, and accommodation becomes submission. We learnt to accommodate power. Our institutions learnt it too. The courts found a doctrine for every occasion: revolutionary legality in 1958, necessity in 1977, validation in 2000. Havel wrote of the greengrocer who displayed a slogan he did not believe because it was safer. Parties became family enterprises; student unions were banned in 1984 and never restored. What we built governs without consent. Pakistan’s next generation will not be formed by protest. It will be formed by argument, and the place to begin it already exists. So what must this generation build first? Not a movement. Character. I have watched men who stood fearlessly at the bar change after reaching the bench. Not suddenly, and not for money. The comfort of office begins quietly to weigh, and each surrender is called realistic. Character is what resists that, and character is built by exposure to lives larger than one’s own. That is what history, literature and poetry are for: to make suffering legible, so that conviction has something to rest upon. But reading alone will not do it. What is read must be argued about, and the structure for that argument is already built, already funded and sitting idle. It is the university classroom. Every class, in every discipline, should be run as a small republic, and the argument should be about the discipline itself. Let the law class argue whether a judgement was rightly decided, not merely what it held. Let the medical class argue triage, consent, and who receives the last bed in a public ward. Let the engineering class argue what was built, who paid, and who must live beside it. Let the business class argue what a wage ought to be, and whether a balance sheet that is lawful is therefore honest. Every syllabus buries such questions beneath what is examinable. Let each class elect its office bearers, for a fixed term and with real duties. Let the elections be contested, and let students lose them, because losing an election and returning next week to sit beside the person who beat you is the most useful hour of civic instruction this country could offer. Let the dissenter be protected by rule, not by the goodwill of the majority. That is how a democratic mind is made: by being outvoted by someone you believe wrong, and having to work beside him afterwards. Argue any of these questions honestly and it will not remain within its discipline. Ask an engineering class whether the dam should be built. The answer requires a lawyer on water rights, an economist on who bears the cost, a doctor on what happens downstream, and someone who has met the people being moved. A faculty can contain a syllabus; it cannot contain a real question. Memorisation keeps a student inside his discipline; argument drives him out. Debate and multidisciplinary education are not two reforms but one, and the first produces the second. This is also where the politics lies. Our professions are organised as separate estates: a bar, a medical association, a chamber of commerce. Each can be managed on its own. What cannot be managed is a generation of doctors, engineers, lawyers and accountants who argued with one another at 20 and still take one another’s calls at 40. Teaching without debate is not education. It is transmission. Education here needs revisiting at its root: less theory recited, more of it tested against the country outside. Take the law class to a district court, the medical class to a public ward at night, the engineering class to the settlement beside the project, the business class to the factory floor. Students must be made to feel Pakistan and its misery, not to read about it. Imagine the young men and women such an education would prepare. The more grounded they are, the more effective they will be. A generation formed this way will not need to be told to push back against unelected power. It will be too many, too competent and too well connected to be governed without consent. None of this arrives quickly. It takes two decades, the time between losing a class election at 20 and running a ministry or a court at 40. That is the honest horizon, and why the work must begin now. Return, then, to the gap. On paper the Constitution is not in doubt: authority exercised through the chosen representatives of the people, rights that power may not violate, public power exercised for the common good. My generation learnt to live inside the distance between that page and this country. Look at what we have brought it to. Closing that distance is the work now left to theirs. They must learn to hold power to account. It begins in a classroom, with an argument, and an election that somebody loses. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. He holds the Distinguished Chair in Constitutionalism & Justice at the Shaikh Ahmad Hassan School of Law, Lums, and is currently a Distinguished Visiting Fellow at Yale University. www.justicemansooralishah.com Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

Pakistan miss out on Asian Games women's cricket final as Athapaththu blitz takes Sri Lanka through. Pakistan missed out on the Asian Games women’ cricket final as Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu’s unbeaten half century gave the side an emphatic eight-wicket victory over Fatima Sana’s charges in the semi-final at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin, Japan on Sunday. Chasing 178, Sri Lanka raced to 178 with 13 balls to spare, with Athapaththu finishing unbeaten on 83 off 50 balls, having struck seven fours and six sixes. Harshitha Samarawickrama was unbeaten on 17. Pakistan had appeared to set a challenging target after posting 177 for four, with Ayesha Zafar top-scoring with 71 off 40 balls and Shawaal Zulfiqar contributing 54 off 50. But Sri Lanka’s chase quickly turned into a one-sided affair, led by their captain’s destructive hitting as Pakistan’s bowlers struggled to contain the scoring rate. It was Pakistan’s second defeat against Sri Lanka in 10 days after the former was knocked out of the recent Women’s Asia Cup as the latter won the tournament’s semi-final. Sri Lanka later lost to India and may meet the Asian champions again in the final if they beat Bangladesh in the second semi-final of the Games. The loser of that match will take on Pakistan for the bronze medal encounter on Tuesday, the same day the final is to be played. Brisk start Sri Lanka made a brisk start despite opening against spin, with Imesha Dulani taking the attack to Umm-e-Hani. They reached 19 without loss after two overs before a costly third over from Momina Riasat, who conceded two no-balls and a wide. Fatima provided Pakistan with their first breakthrough in the fifth over, having Dulani bowled for 27 off 21 balls. Sri Lanka were 39 for one at that stage. Athapaththu, initially watchful, then accelerated spectacularly. She hit Momina for a six, four, six and four in the eighth over to take Sri Lanka to 70 for one. The Sri Lankan captain continued her assault, striking Nashra Sandhu for two fours and a six in the 10th over. Hasini Perera joined in the acceleration, particularly against Tuba Hassan, and Sri Lanka moved to 121 for one after 13 overs, needing 57 from 42 balls. Nashra eventually broke the partnership in the following over when Hasini, who had reached 42 off 26 balls with three fours and three sixes, was caught by Umm-e-Hani at cover. Sri Lanka were 131 for two with 47 still required from 36 deliveries. There was little further resistance from Pakistan. Athapaththu moved to 65 off 44 balls after Fatima’s return over went for 11, before taking 15 from Umm-e-Hani’s final over, including consecutive sixes. Sri Lanka were 157 for two after 16 overs and needed only 21 from the final four overs. Pakistan were also unable to hold on to a chance when Aliya Riaz dropped Athapaththu at long-off off Ayesha Zafar with the batter on 79. Athapaththu hit a four in the same over before completing the chase with two balls of the 18th over remaining. Ayesha stars Earlier, Pakistan’s innings had suffered an early setback when opener Gull Feroza was clean bowled by Sugandika Kumari off the second delivery. Saira Jabeen and Shawaal steadied the innings, but Saira fell for a brisk 17 off 14 balls when Sri Lanka captain Athapaththu had her caught at deep midwicket in the sixth over. Ayesha then joined Shawaal and took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers. The pair added 115 runs, with Ayesha particularly aggressive against the spin. She reached her half-century off just 27 balls as Pakistan crossed 100 in the 12th over. Ayesha eventually fell for a 40-ball 71, including nine fours and two sixes, when a risky single resulted in a run-out at the bowler’s end in the 17th over. Shawaal brought up her half-century from 47 balls, having struck three fours and two sixes, but was dismissed for 54 off 50 balls in the following over, caught at deep midwicket after failing to get enough power behind a shot. Fatima provided the late impetus with an unbeaten 20 off 12 balls, including two fours and a six, while Eyman Fatima struck a four from the final delivery to take Pakistan to 177 for four. Pakistan’s innings was also helped by several fielding lapses from Sri Lanka, who missed opportunities during the middle overs. Kumari, Athapaththu and Kawya Kavindi took one wicket apiece for Sri Lanka, with Kumari the most economical of the three, conceding 31 runs from her four overs.

Turkiye says it could help meet Saudi Arabia’s military needs. ANKARA: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis and that Turkiye was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that includes Pakistan. “We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, sovereignty. We have an alliance agreement in our pact. We are in serious solidarity on this point. They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these,” Fidan told broadcaster NTV . The joint defence agreement, signed last month, stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them. The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, have been launching attacks on Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July. The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, threatening global oil supplies and the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted. President Donald Trump has rebuffed pleas from the Saudis for military support to fight the Houthis, who agreed a ceasefire with the United States last year after Washington bombed the group for two months. Fidan said that it was unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be made a part of the US-Iran war as it had no desire to join the conflict. He added, without elaborating, that proposals have been conveyed to all sides to end the fighting. “There are many initiatives, but the sides need to accept these,” he said. “There are new proposals, I hope they accept them. Otherwise, the crisis was tolerated until a certain point, but the economic reflections have started to exceed the point of being tolerable.” Turkiye, which has Nato’s second-largest army, has said the pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia was open to expansion and did not seek to replace any existing alliances. Earlier on Saturday, Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city’s main airport. Turkiye has condemned the Houthi attacks and called for them to stop immediately. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026
