KP CM Afridi blames deteriorating security situation on ‘failed’ foreign policy. PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Saturday said that the deteriorating security situation in the country was the result of a failed foreign policy pursued over the last 22 years. “If a policy is not delivering results and is continuously failing, there is a need to change it,” he said during a visit to Kohat. The chief minister met the families of the police personnel and civilians martyred in the terrorist attack on the Police Lines and paid tribute to the police, counter-terrorism department, Special Branch, Rescue 1122, doctors, district administration and the people of Kohat for their courage and resilience, according to an official statement issued here. The chief minister said that the manner in which the security personnel and other responders confronted terrorists during an operation lasting nearly 20 hours was highly commendable. Sympathises with families of police officials, civilians martyred in Kohat blast He said the police personnel and civilians who lost lives while confronting terrorists had made the ultimate sacrifice for the protection of the nation. Mr Afridi said Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been fighting terrorism continuously since 2004, spanning nearly 22 years, during which the province had lost more than 80,000 lives. He said that the government that came to power in Afghanistan was welcomed with celebrations by the “bogus and imposed” Pakistani rulers but the situation later turned bad. “Our trade [with Afghanistan] has been disrupted; the border has been closed; economic activities in the tribal districts have come to a standstill, and terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa continues to rise,” he said. The chief minister said the closure of the Afghan border had caused Khyber Pakhtunkhwa losses of more than Rs8 billion during the previous financial year, while the province was likely to face further economic losses during the current financial year. He said if a policy was not delivering results and was continuously failing, there was a need to change it. Mr Afridi said that the people and police of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa continued to bear the immense burden of the fight against terrorism. He said that police personnel remained on the frontline, fighting, sustaining injuries and laying down their lives, while innocent citizens, with no crime or wrongdoing to their name, continued to be killed and injured. The chief minister said despite those sacrifices, the people of the province continued to be viewed in that manner, which was deeply regrettable. Referring to the prevailing state narrative, he said that those imposed on the people were calling them terrorists while claiming that there is no threat from India. Mr Afridi said that the federal government and institutions were trying to suppress PTI’s political activity instead of addressing the challenge of terrorism. He said that while the focus of the federal government and institutions was on such matters, there was little concern for the people who were making sacrifices on the frontline. Addressing the youth, people and police of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the chief minister said that no one else would come to stand with them and that they must stand up for themselves, their people, their province and the country. He urged them to remain steadfast and keep their morale high, noting that the people and police of the province have continued to fight terrorism with courage and determination for the past 22 years without allowing their resolve to break. Mr Afridi announced that financial assistance would also be provided to the families of those martyred in the incident who didn’t fall within the scope of the government’s Shuhada Package. Announcing the provision of modern medical equipment at the District Headquarters Hospital in Kohat, he said that the shortage of CT scan, MRI and other essential modern medical equipment would be addressed. The chief minister said that DHQ hospitals across the province were being revamped and that necessary modern equipment would be provided to the hospital. He also announced the establishment of a police station for the Special Branch in Kohat and said that the project would be completed at the earliest. Mr Afridi said that patient care at the Kohat Police Hospital should be improved with the help of necessary facilities. He also took note of the shortage of police personnel and said that the matter would be taken up in the cabinet for necessary decisions. Earlier, the chief minister visited the Kohat District Headquarters Hospital, met the injured blast victims and wished them speedy recovery. Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

MQM-P wants administrative restructuring of Sindh without altering boundaries: Mustafa Kamal. • Alleges 18th Amendment divided country into ‘four independent states’ • At separate presser, Farooq Sattar claims Sindh to have six administrative units soon KARACHI: Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan leader and Federal Health Minister Syed Mustafa Kamal has said his party wants “administrative restructuring of Sindh without altering its boundaries”. “We want administrative units with their own assemblies and chief executives, where National Finance Commission [NFC] funds are directly transferred,” he told a press conference here at the party’s temporary headquarters in Bahadurabad on Saturday. However, the absence of party chairman Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui and senior leader Dr Farooq Sattar from Mr Kamal’s press conference suggested that the party’s internal rifts over leadership control are far from over. In the evening, Dr Sattar held a separate press conference, conspicuous by Mr Kamal’s absence, where he announced a rally to be held on Sunday (today) and claimed that six administrative units would soon be created in Sindh. At the first press conference, Mr Kamal said that the 18th Amendment had practically divided the country into “four independent states” and the MQM-P wanted to unite the country through the creation of new administrative units. Accompanied by senior leader Anis Kaimkhani and others, he made it clear that whoever leads the campaign for administrative units — whether a person, institution, or ruler — will be their hero for saving Pakistan. “The PPP is furious [over new administrative units] because they realise the sun is setting on their power and the public will now hold them accountable,” he said, accusing the ruling party of “conspiring to associate the entire Sindhi nation with some corrupt beneficiaries of the current system”. Mr Kamal said that the PPP can no longer hide its bad governance behind the so-called Sindh card, nor can it “engineer Sindhi-Mohajir riots”. “If bloodshed was bound to happen, it would have occurred over the spread of HIV/AIDS among children via infected syringes at Valika Hospital, Karachi and Larkana; the denial of drinking water; innocent people being crushed under dumpers; deaths from falling into open manholes; citizens being murdered for Rs10,000 mobile phones; the denial of government jobs; the selling of urban Sindh’s quota on fake domiciles; and rampant bribery in every government department,” he said. “Just past Hyderabad, the interior of Sindh tells a tragic tale of destruction, devastation and corruption. MQM-Pakistan is fighting the case of these oppressed Sindhis. We assure Sindhi nation that after the formation of administrative units, their lives, property and honour will be far more secure than today,” he said. Commenting on remarks made by a senior PPP leader against Field Marshal Asim Munir, he said it “exposed the ruling party’s malice, hatred and enmity towards institutions”. “The time has come for the state to decide whether to save Pakistan or cater to the whims of the PPP,” he said. Strongly condemning the attacks on Saudi Arabia, Mr Kamal said that every worker of his party was ready to sacrifice their life for the protection and sanctity of Makkah and Madina. “We have defence pacts with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, and whatever decision the state makes in this regard, we will fully support it,” he said. MQM-P to stage rally today Later in the day, senior MQM-P leader Dr Farooq Sattar told another press conference that six administrative units are going to be created in Sindh very soon. Although he did not elaborate, his remarks seem to suggest that he was talking about Sindh’s existing six divisions — Karachi, Hyderabad, Suk­kur, Larkana, Mirpur­khas and Shaheed Benazir­abad. He said the MQM-P was organising a rally on Sunday (today) from Ayesha Manzil to Mazar-i-Quaid in favour of the demand for new administrative units and provinces in the country. He said that for the past 18 years, the public has been deprived of an empowered local government system and education, health and employment facilities. “When the system of governance fails, the transfer of authority and power to the grassroots level becomes mandatory; therefore, we are talking about establishing new administrative units,” he said. He appealed to citizens belonging to all ethnic and linguistic backgrounds, particularly youths, to participate in large numbers in the rally and play their full role against the status quo. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/11/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 11 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. What Future for Venezuela after the U.S. Oil Carve-up? pzeiler Fri, 09/11/2026 - 11:11 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List US Energy Secretary Chris Wright (L) and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez (R) talk during a meeting over an oil agreement at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas on September 2, 2026. Juan Barreto / AFP Q&A / Latin America & Caribbean 11 September 2026 17 minutes What Future for Venezuela after the U.S. Oil Carve-up? The Trump administration has announced an agreement with Caracas that it says gives the U.S. a major stake in the Venezuelan oil industry. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts Phil Gunson and Delaney Simon explore the reported deal’s ramifications. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Español Español English Related Tags Venezuela United States What happened? U.S. President Donald Trump announced on 28 August that his administration had reached an agreement that purportedly gives Washington control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves, in what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”. According to Trump, the 100-year concession – to be run by a private company under de facto U.S. government control – would more than double U.S. reserves, permit the U.S. to replenish its strategic stockpiles and alleviate pressure on fuel prices. The White House emphasised that the deal would come at no cost to the U.S. taxpayer. Venezuela’s government confirmed the arrangement, while offering conflicting details as to its duration and precise terms. The announcement is one more sign that the relationship between Caracas and Washington has mutated into one of diminished Venezuelan sovereignty and informal U.S. dominion, with a stress on extracting Venezuela’s natural resources. On 3 January, just hours after U.S. special forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, whisking them to New York for trial on drug trafficking charges, Trump promised that the U.S. would “run” Venezuela and take “a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground”. To replace Maduro, the U.S. endorsed former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez to be interim leader, making clear that her hold on the post would depend on staying in Trump’s good graces. [The U.S.] has brokered the greater part of [Venezuela’s] oil exports, channelling the proceeds into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury. While the U.S. avoided the potentially disastrous fallout of dismantling the chavista regime in Caracas without a viable alternative, Washington has since swung to the other extreme of giving full backing to Rodríguez, in the process tightening its grip on Venezuela and its raw materials. It has brokered the greater part of the country’s oil exports, channelling the proceeds into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury, which decides how and when the revenue is spent. In late January, weeks after Maduro was arraigned in a U.S. court, Venezuela’s interim government also passed a sweeping reform intended to draw foreign investors into the oil and gas industry by reducing tax and royalties due to the state, while allowing greater private participation in oil production. Despite the overhaul of the legal regime and the transformation of Venezuela-U.S. relations – which had been prickly under the late President Hugo Chávez (1999-2013) and downright hostile under Maduro’s authoritarian rule – the Trump administration has struggled to convince U.S. oil majors to invest more in Venezuela. Dilapidated infrastructure, including a crumbling electrical grid, will require years of costly repairs if new hydrocarbons operations in the country are to generate major profits. Investors are also concerned by the absence of rule of law and fear that any agreement reached with the de facto authorities could be reversed if they were to be overthrown or replaced by a democratically elected government. Frustrated by big oil’s reticence to dive into Venezuela, and under growing pressure ahead of U.S. midterm elections to lower gasoline prices as the Middle East war nudges them higher, the Trump administration has looked for alternative routes to boosting output. Both Rodríguez and Trump indicated that under the new agreement, seventeen oilfields would be developed, requiring an investment of $100 billion, and fattening the Venezuelan exchequer to the tune of more than $200 billion overall. Rodríguez, however, gave a markedly different account of some of the deal’s key terms. According to the Venezuelan leader, the agreement is to last for 25, not 100 years, and it does not involve relinquishing Venezuelan sovereign control of oil reserves. But the agreement’s text has not been made public; not even the Venezuelan parliament has seen it. Critics have therefore persisted in calling the deal an astonishing handover of strategic resources, one that may violate the Venezuelan constitution and that lacks clear guarantees of economic benefit for Venezuelans. What do we know about the deal’s contents? While the terms remain opaque, U.S. officials have said the arrangement gives Washington preferential purchasing rights and a 35 per cent stake in a private company that would operate the seventeen oilfields under a century-long lease. Roughly half these fields are in the Lake Maracaibo basin, the north-western area where the Venezuelan oil industry began over a century ago, but whose facilities are in a state of severe disrepair . The other half lie in the Orinoco Belt, just north of the Orinoco River in central Venezuela, where development would in some cases require building new roads, as well as housing, production facilities and pipelines. All the oilfields in Venezuela are state property. Washington would not control the fields directly, but would instead wield influence through a private company, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), which now operates three of the seventeen fields and would hold the concessions to all of them . The U.S. State Department would have the right to purchase at production cost 20 per cent of the oil produced by all current and future fields run by NABEP. It would also have the right of “first refusal” on the remaining 80 per cent of production, giving the U.S. government the chance to buy oil ahead of any other customer. The Trump administration says it will have veto power in appointing the NABEP’s parent company’s board of directors, which appears not to exist yet. It also says a majority of members will have to be U.S. citizens. The U.S. government is no stranger to state-owned enterprises – it is involved in corporations that run everything from regional power grids (like the Tennessee Valley Authority) to rail (for example, Amtrak) and mail delivery (the U.S. Postal Service) – but such a level of control of another country’s natural resources, enabled by U.S. military action and secured through U.S. political influence, has not been common practice since Washington exercised quasi-colonial rule over various Latin American nations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In more recent history, the U.S. government has taken equity stakes in companies during crises – for example, to bail out the auto industry after the 2008 financial crisis. But, as a former Pentagon official told Crisis Group, there appears to be no comparable public interest reason to take a stake in NABEP. “They’re doing it because they can get away with it … and they are trying to take the oil”. The White House has named the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to hold the equity stakes in NABEP, a move that conceals a complicated legal picture. The office, which was established in December 2022 under President Joe Biden to stimulate investment in technologies seen as critical to national security, is not currently authorised by Congress to take equity stakes in private companies. But its director, who performs another function as the senior advisor to the deputy secretary of defense , seems to have invoked the authority of the Pentagon’s Office of Industrial Base Policy, which is authorised to hold equity. Whether the Pentagon has the legal authority to act in this way is debatable; it is up to Congress to consider the matter. The Trump administration appears to have used a financial tool called “penny warrants” to structure its equity stake. In any event, the Trump administration appears to have used a financial tool called “penny warrants” to structure its equity stake. This instrument would give the U.S. the opportunity to purchase stock in NABEP for a nominal price at a certain point in the future, an arrangement that could give Washington a steep discount once the stock appreciates, entitle it to dividends and afford it substantial control of the company’s future. Under the Trump administration, the Pentagon has expanded the precedent of using these warrants when making loans, allowing the government to later sell them, potentially for a profit – operating, in effect, like a venture capital firm. The opacity of the deal, along with suspicions that certain private-sector interests are being favoured thanks to their government ties in Caracas, Washington or both, have stirred additional concerns. The U.S. Congress was on legislative recess at the time of the announcement, and reactions, mostly on social media, have split largely along party lines, with Republicans generally supportive and Democrats flagging concerns. Florida Republicans, who are up for re-election in districts with large Venezuelan diaspora communities, were somewhat cautious, emphasising the need for free and fair elections. On the other hand, Democrats who have been sceptical of the administration’s aims in Venezuela have criticised the deal on grounds of potential corruption . Among other issues, NABEP is run by Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan businessman who has faced multiple investigations at home and abroad for alleged embezzlement of Venezuelan state funds and is linked to Rodríguez’s government (more below). What does the U.S. administration want from this deal? The agreement comes at a time when President Trump is facing declining poll numbers , criticism of his handling of foreign policy ( in particular his conduct of the Middle East war) and growing concerns about his economic management. Voters worry about the cost of living, especially fuel prices, with diesel hitting a new record high, surging over 55 per cent since the war began. According to the latest polling, Democrats are in contention to win control of both the House and the Senate in midterm elections, which are widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term. Faced with these political headwinds, Trump has returned to his long-running fixation with “taking the oil” in his approach to U.S. foreign relations. (One of Trump’s critiques of the 2003 Iraq war was precisely that the U.S. did not assume control of the country’s fossil fuels.) The administration has boasted that this deal will secure “U.S. energy dominance for the next century” and even boost the country’s economic growth, as the crude would be “processed through U.S. refineries and pumped with American rigs and infrastructure”. The oil derived from the agreement would, according to the White House , supply the military and serve “other sensitive uses”. In the long run, it could also theoretically provide barrels for the U.S. consumer market and allow domestic production to refill the country’s strategic oil reserve, which is now at its lowest point since 1983. The agreement with Venezuela, however, may fail to meet these sunny predictions of a spurt in oil production. While the fields assigned to NABEP supposedly represent 65 billion barrels of recoverable oil, the figure is based on a highly optimistic 20 per cent recovery rate, the term for what portion of the oil in a given deposit can reasonably be extracted over its lifetime. According to Venezuelan oil specialist Francisco Monaldi, the true figure is likely nearer one third of that. (If the higher estimates are correct, Saudi Aramco would be the only private company in the world controlling larger oil reserves than NABEP, according to U.S. officials.) Economists are in broad agreement that Venezuela’s oil industry would need tens of billions of dollars in investment ... to restore production to historical levels. Moreover, any major increase in Venezuelan oil production would not be achieved in the near future – and certainly not before the U.S. midterm elections. Venezuela currently produces between 800,000 and 900,000 barrels a day, compared to over three million barrels a day in the first decade of the 21st century. NABEP is pumping about 200,000 barrels per day, and Washington appears to have chosen Betancourt as a partner precisely because he has the contacts and risk tolerance to advance difficult projects. Yet even the rosiest projections, assuming rapid efforts to rehabilitate existing oilfields and infrastructure, suggest that a minimum of two years will be required before the deal will generate new streams of revenue. Around half the identified potential projects involve “greenfield” or undeveloped sites, some of them “in the middle of nowhere”, as an oil company representative told Crisis Group. Economists are in broad agreement that Venezuela’s oil industry would need tens of billions of dollars in investment and nearly a decade of work to restore production to historical levels. Since the U.S. government says it will not be putting up the money (as noted, the administration has stressed that the deal is cost-free for U.S. taxpayers), and the only private company so far involved, NABEP, does not have it, it remains unclear where that investment will come from. The Washington Post reported that Betancourt may seek advance payments from oil traders up front, based on anticipated later revenue. But major oil corporations seem unlikely to work with NABEP directly, given the judicial cases against Betancourt and concerns about the agreement’s legality in Venezuela. A number of them, however, have been negotiating their own concessions with the Rodríguez government, focusing either on gas or on the expansion of existing operations. Chevron Corporation, which remained in Venezuela while many others left, announced on 2 September that it would work through its Venezuelan joint ventures to develop new fields adjacent to its existing operations, with the aim of doubling its Venezuela output to 600,000 barrels a day over the next five years, according to the oil firm . After 3 January, the U.S. gave commodity traders Vitol Group and Trafigura Group the contracts to place Venezuelan oil on the international market, though soon afterward Washington opened the business to other traders. More recently, several refiners have begun to deal directly with the Venezuelan state oil corporation PDVSA, bypassing the middlemen. Beyond the oil itself, the administration describes the deal as “reasserting the Monroe Doctrine”, which it understands as ensuring U.S. hegemony in the Western Hemisphere. So far, its efforts to cement U.S. dominance have included cultivating political allies, boosting its stakes in the region’s natural resources and critical minerals, and encouraging regional military cooperation aimed at stemming the flows of drugs and migrants northward. As part of the latter, a campaign against small boats allegedly trafficking narcotics on both the Pacific and Caribbean seaboards, deemed by a critical mass of legal scholars to involve extrajudicial killings, had claimed at least 227 lives as of early September . Trump’s application of the doctrine is also explicit in seeking to push other global powers out of positions of influence in Latin America. The White House says NABEP would operate oilfields previously controlled or serviced by Russian and Chinese firms. In response, the Chinese government demanded that its “legitimate rights and interests” be respected. Beijing is still believed to be owed over $10 billion from past credit offered Venezuela; this debt was largely being paid in kind, through oil shipments, before 3 January. Russia has previously decried what a Kremlin spokesman called “blatant discrimination” against it, and in February the Russian state-owned oil company Roszarubezhneft promised to defend its legal claims. What do Venezuelans think? Criticism, much of it impassioned, has come from across the political spectrum. Venezuelans have questioned not only the ties with NABEP, but also the deal’s lack of transparency and the fact that it was announced without input from the Venezuelan people and in the absence of legitimately elected authorities. Even those inclined to support the arrangement concede that it is hard to defend without full disclosure of its terms. Many ordinary Venezuelans have told Crisis Group of their shock and dismay at the public statements describing its parameters. Left-wing opponents of the Rodríguez government, who argue that the interim president is betraying the legacy of the founder of the ruling chavista movement, former President Chávez, staged a small but noisy march in central Caracas on 29 August to protest the deal. Chávez’s long-time oil minister Rafael Ramírez, who is exiled in Italy and faces corruption allegations (which he denies) back home, called it a “neocolonial” arrangement and a “ dagger to the heart ” of Venezuela. Economists associated with both the moderate and hard-line wings of the opposition also questioned the deal. Harvard professor Ricardo Hausmann, a former Venezuelan planning minister and supporter of exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado, called it “ shameful ” and “illegitimate”. Machado herself was initially silent. While she has expressed her support for the Trump administration’s intervention in Venezuela and long championed the full privatisation of the oil industry, she and her movement Vente Venezuela have not challenged the concept of state ownership of oil reserves; they have instead insisted that any restructuring of the industry be carried out by a democratically elected government. On 3 September, Machado broke her silence, releasing a seven-minute video in which she describes the “sadness [and] anger” the announcement provoked, and spoke of “deep concern” about its implications, though without mentioning Trump by name. The chequered history of NABEP’s owner, Alejandro Betancourt, is a particular source of concern. Few if any private individuals are more closely associated in the minds of Venezuelans with the alleged embezzlement of public funds than Betancourt. As a young businessman, he founded Derwick Associates, which in 2011 obtained a series of no-bid contracts worth around $5 billion to build power stations amid a nationwide electricity shortage. The company appears to have taken the up-front payments but failed to resolve the problem; Venezuela today suffers from its most severe blackouts ever. Amid this cacophony of objections, the opposition team hand-picked by Washington for political transition talks with the Rodríguez government, led by 2015 National Assembly chair Dinorah Figuera, has found it hard to respond publicly. Neither Figuera’s faction nor Machado’s seems to have been consulted on the deal before it was made public. Is the deal legal? Several aspects of the agreement appear to run afoul of Venezuelan law. While the reported arrangement includes a 100-year concession, Article 12 of the country’s constitution declares the country’s oil deposits public property, and as such inalienable, while Article 302 grants the state the exclusive right to exploit them. Even under the sweeping oil law reform that came into force earlier in 2026, private ownership (as opposed to operational control) of an oilfield is not allowed, and an initial concession cannot exceed 25 years. In her public statements, Rodríguez has insisted that the agreement in no way infringes upon Venezuela’s sovereign rights, without offering details. Another source of legal jeopardy is the status of the Rodríguez government itself. The acting president, who has never held elected office, owes her position to the 3 January U.S. military incursion that ousted Maduro and installed her in power. Venezuela’s parliament, the National Assembly – which endorsed the oil accord on 1 September without having seen the full text – is chaired by Rodríguez’s brother Jorge and largely acts as a rubber stamp for the executive. (Opposition legislators of the small Libertad caucus abstained from voting on the agreement, saying they needed to see the actual text.) The U.S. government has described the 2025 legislative elections as a “sham”. Indeed, the Trump administration continues to recognise the rump of the opposition-dominated 2016-2021 parliament (known as the 2015 Assembly, for the year it was elected) as the only surviving democratic institution in the country. Under the Venezuelan constitution, the acts of any official or branch of the state considered to have “usurped” authority are rendered null and void. The eventual restoration of constitutional normality and the rule of law in Venezuela would thus open the very real possibility of a legal challenge to the agreement, even if a new government was not opposed to the deal. What does this mean for Venezuela’s future? Since the 3 January raid, the Trump administration has assumed a dominant role in determining Venezuela’s political and economic trajectory, with the U.S. president even suggesting that it could become the 51st state. Washington’s stranglehold on the country’s foreign earnings, and the explicit threat of further military action if Caracas defies its will, leave Rodríguez little room for manoeuvre. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described Washington’s three-phase plan for Venezuela as involving stabilisation, economic recovery and political transition. Yet far from pushing for a fresh presidential election to make amends for the last poll fraudulently won by Maduro in July 2024, Trump has repeatedly expressed his satisfaction with the current set-up, describing Rodríguez as “highly respected” and giving her government glowing praise. In late July, Trump declared that Venezuela was “ not ready yet ” for elections. With terms that appear designed to favour U.S. interests over those of Venezuelans, which depend on Caracas’s compliance, and which would likely prove unacceptable to a freely elected government, this deal further reduces the incentives for the White House to seek democratic change in Venezuela. The deal also complicates efforts by the opposition to push for a genuine political transition. Washington has compelled the Rodríguez government to sit down to talks with an opposition delegation led by Dinorah Figuera on political reform. Those talks began in August, producing an initial agreement on change at the Supreme Court. Negotiations are due to resume in mid-September, with a focus on political rights and reform of the electoral authority. But the opposition delegation representing the 2015 Assembly has little leverage beyond its U.S. backing. It already suffers from a perceived deficit of legitimacy, and its reputation may be further tarnished by association with an unpopular deal that the delegation was not consulted on but may lack the autonomy to repudiate. Machado is also in a bind. She has repeatedly sought to return to Venezuela, only to be blocked by the Trump-Rodríguez alliance. Neither confrontation with Trump nor blind obedience will further Machado’s calls for a quick and free presidential vote that would likely cement her status as pre-eminent opposition leader and might see her emerge victorious. In her video message about the deal, Machado reiterated that she views the U.S. as “the principal partner Venezuela needs” but added that agreements of this magnitude require “solid institutions”, not arbitrary assignations. She repeated her call for free elections as soon as possible. Some Venezuelans say they would be prepared to accept the loss of sovereignty in exchange for greater political freedom and an improvement in economic conditions. Some Venezuelans say they would be prepared to accept the loss of sovereignty in exchange for greater political freedom and an improvement in economic conditions for a country that has been mired in a humanitarian emergency for well over a decade. Needs have only grown more acute following twin earthquakes in June that the UN estimates added 700,000 individuals to the list of those in need of basic assistance. But neither freedom nor economic relief appear guaranteed within the compass of the current arrangement between Caracas and Washington. More broadly, the overall terms of the post-3 January relationship between the U.S. and Venezuela give serious cause for concern. Washington’s direct control of key pieces of Venezuela’s economy and its outsized influence over its government have led Caracas to loosen its shackles on political dissent but have also created a set of perverse incentives that seem to be hindering progress toward a genuine democratic opening. Venezuela’s politicians and business leaders are obliged to appeal first and foremost to the Trump administration rather than to any domestic constituency. Trump, meanwhile, has made quite explicit his view that the Venezuela operation is a blueprint for Latin America and beyond, combining military force, economic coercion and resource extraction. Regardless of whether administration officials still imagine a medium- to long-term plan for a democratic transition, for now Washington appears determined to grab what it can before Venezuelans can once more exercise their right to govern themselves. An Historic Poll Puts Peace to the Test in the Philippines cthuratong Fri, 09/11/2026 - 17:10 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Campaign posters in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht Q&A / Asia-Pacific 11 September 2026 12 minutes An Historic Poll Puts Peace to the Test in the Philippines In mid-September, residents of the Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines will elect regional parliamentary representatives. In this Q&A, Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht explains the importance of this step in the peace process between the national government and ex-rebels in the region. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Georgi Engelbrecht Senior Analyst, Philippines https://twitter.com/Durian_Diaries Related Tags Philippines What is happening? On 14 September, over two million residents of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao will elect their parliament for the first time. The vote is a milestone in the implementation of the 2014 peace accord, which ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists. In 2019, a parliament was created to govern the Bangsamoro, with Philippine presidents appointing its members. Slightly more than half the seats were reserved for members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, or MILF, the region’s largest Moro Muslim armed movement. Following four postponements of the vote over the last seven years – first because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and later due to a range of legal and political complications – residents will finally have the chance to elect all their regional parliamentary representatives. The fact that the vote is now taking place is an accomplishment in and of itself. Election fever has gripped the region since the campaign officially began in late July. Vehicles roam the streets with loudspeakers blasting party jingles, huge posters of candidates decorate Bangsamoro roads, and catchy slogans and vlogs saturate citizens’ social media feeds. With voters set to choose from twelve parties, and with 631 candidates jockeying for 80 parliamentary seats, the competition to attract public support has been fierce. Electioneering has a darker side, too, with some campaigns spreading disinformation about rival candidates and parties. The vote is set to deliver a long-awaited verdict on how well MILF candidates have handled the transition from conducting guerrilla warfare to administering the autonomous region. Over the last seven years, the MILF-led interim administration has achieved a number of modest results, for instance strengthening social services and reducing child mortality. That said, and despite residents’ high expectations at the start of the peace process, the people of the Bangsamoro are still among the poorest in the country. The elections also come at a moment of high tension within the movement’s ranks. In March 2025, the national government replaced Chief Minister Murad Ebrahim, the MILF’s chairman, with the movement’s top military commander Abdulraof Macacua, generating a schism in the organisation. During an assembly in early September, the Central Committee stripped Macacua and 40 other MILF military commanders of their official functions. Mohagher Iqbal, head of the peace implementation panel and MILF vice chair, remains loyal to the displaced chief minister, Murad. Who is taking part in the polls? Twelve political parties are competing. While some have laid out clear platforms, the majority have had little of substance to offer in their campaigns. Such is often the case in the Philippines, where political campaigns tend to centre around personalities, rather than policy platforms, given the weaknesses of the party system. Even so, a milestone in the Bangsamoro’s political life came on 27 August, when representatives from all parties took part in a six-hour public debate in Cotabato City on priorities for the future government. Broadly speaking, the political spectrum can be divided into three blocs. The first is made up of the ex-rebels, who are represented by three parties broadly reflecting the split at the heights of the MILF: the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), which is a vehicle for Murad; the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which is led by Macacua but includes several senior MILF cadres and influential local politicians; and the ABOT party, which is comprised of Iqbal partisans. In addition to the troika of parties affiliated with the MILF, two parties have emerged from the Moro National Liberation Front, the Bangsamoro’s first separatist movement (from which the MILF split in 1977). Campaign posters of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht The second category consists of parties led by the region’s political clans, or families that dominate local politics and aspire to extend their reach across the region. The most notable is the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition, an alliance of powerful clan leaders associated with the Alonto-Adiong, Hataman and Mangudadatu families, whose members felt politically excluded during the MILF-led interim administration. Once the primary opposition to the ex-rebels, this coalition now faces competition from the Bangsamoro Federalist Party mentioned above, as well as the Progressive Bangsamoro Party, whose base is in the provinces of Sulu and Tawi-Tawi. The latter is linked to the Loong and Matba families. A third category encompasses smaller parties. Some of these are led by civil society figures who promise institutional reform and champion minority rights. The Raayat Party, for example, includes experienced lawyers and legislators who are pressing for transparency in government and better access to public services. The Indigenous, Settler, Sama and Minorities Alliance Party, which focuses on safeguarding the rights and interests of the region’s Sama minority, is also among the smaller parties that would bring valuable expertise and perspectives to the parliament. These two parties are, however, unlikely to win more than a handful of seats . Half the parliamentary seats will be filled via proportional representation, with voters casting ballots for party lists. Citizens across the region’s 32 electoral districts will also vote for district representatives, who will fill another 40 per cent of the seats. The remaining 10 per cent (eight seats) are reserved for “sectors”, also elected by popular vote – except in the case of non-Moro Indigenous communities, whose representatives have already been elected via community assemblies . Non-Moro Indigenous communities and Christian settlers will each hold two seats, while women, traditional leaders, youth and religious scholars (known as ulama ) will have one seat each. Once the elected parliamentarians take office on 30 October, they will elect the chief minister through a majority vote. Unless a single party wins more than 41 seats – an unlikely prospect – party leaders will therefore need to forge a coalition in order to form a government. Some locals suspect that President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr.’s administration favours an outcome that would preserve Macacua as leader, with his MILF faction governing in a coalition with dominant local clans. This suspicion is not unfounded, given the national government’s unexpected move in 2025 to place Macacua at the helm of the Bangsamoro government. Campaign posters of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party and the Bangsamoro Party in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht How has the campaign played out? The UBJP has campaigned hard. Its strategy consists of harnessing grassroots support while building alliances with politicians who oppose the Grand Coalition and the Federalist Party. Leaders and senior cadres emphasise the importance of honouring the 2014 peace agreement in full. In rallies across the region, UBJP candidates have called for “moral governance”, a concept that infuses the notion of good governance with Islamic principles. Other parties also invoke religious language, but the UBJP is the only one using it as a pillar of its campaign. The Federalist Party, meanwhile, has focused on a message of “inclusion” and anti-corruption, while the parties associated with the MNLF highlight their movement’s early contribution to the Moro struggle. The Grand Coalition, for its part, is leveraging its clan-based network, which is led by the governors of Lanao del Sur and Basilan. The campaign has revealed an inherent contradiction at the heart of Bangsamoro politics. That is, despite the establishment of a parliamentary system – which is distinct from the presidential system used by the Philippines at the national level – and the concomitant creation of new political parties, clans and personalities still matter more than parties or issues. Established political families can leverage patronage, largesse and the campaign experience they have acquired thanks to national and local polls to garner voters’ support. Familial ties still shape party lists, and some clans are fielding candidates from different parties in order to ensure that they are installed in the region’s power structure no matter the vote’s outcome. “The electoral game, the innovations of the system, have already been rigged”, a former party aide lamented. Are conditions in place for a peaceful election? Electoral violence constitutes the biggest threat to these polls. Flare-ups are a staple of Philippine politics, and election-related murders are regular occurrences. The presence of armed groups and widespread proliferation of firearms mean that political violence is even more widespread in the Bangsamoro. In the Philippines’ 2025 elections for governors, mayors and national senators, more than a third of the violent incidents recorded nationwide took place in the Bangsamoro. In one incident during the mayoral election in the town of Hadji Mohammad Ajul in Basilan, a clash between warring clans claimed four lives. The Philippine Commission on Elections has designated almost 40 per cent of the region’s towns as being at high risk of violence. Multiple incidents have already occurred since the beginning of the campaign – including an attempted ambush on interim Chief Minister Macacua. It is, however, unclear who was behind the attack. Indeed, many locals believe it may have been staged in order to engender sympathy for Macacua and boost his Federalist Party’s chances. Direct clashes of the military and police with ex-rebels are unlikely, but shootouts and disturbances involving competing political camps and candidates are possible, including on election day. Two main risks stand out. First, contests for district seats – which involve individual candidates facing off against one another – can more easily tip into violence given the personal nature of the competition. Secondly, friction could arise between supporters of the UBJP and the Federalist Party, both of them offshoots of the ex-rebel MILF, as well as between the UBJP and the Grand Coalition, particularly in areas where all the major political forces are campaigning. Those who seek to threaten or attack rivals can deploy tried-and-tested tactics ranging from bombings on the eve of the polls to scare voters to attacks on polling booths. Crisis Group knows of at least one powerbroker who has allegedly prepositioned dozens of rifles in a Maguindanaon village. Inflammatory online posts and trolling, often involving prominent MILF-linked personalities representing different factions, could also help spur real-world violence. A young cadre warned that this escalation is “just a matter of time”. Campaign rhetoric has on occasion turned worryingly bellicose. During a Federalist Party rally in August, Macacua said the party “was prepared for war to ensure that the Bangsamoro is on the right path”. Though he did not specify the target of this warning, some locals perceived it as a threat to his former comrades. On 3 August, top MILF military leader Abdullah Macapaar – alias Commander Bravo, who remains loyal to the Central Committee – warned that opponents of his party might manipulate the polls. The following month, after state authorities intercepted MILF members under his command and sent them back to their camp, he declared in a speech: “If we are picked on, we will not allow ourselves to be bullied”. In terms of potential flashpoints, the greatest security risks lie in the province of Maguindanao del Sur and the Special Geographic Area, a cluster of eight municipalities near the regional capital of Cotabato City. In these locations, candidates include prominent MILF personalities and commanders, as well as traditional elites. For example, the son of MILF chair Murad Ebrahim will face off against Butch Malang, a senior MILF commander widely considered loyal to Chief Minister Macacua. Meanwhile, parts of Lanao del Sur province, which has a long history of political violence, are also vulnerable to flare-ups. The island province of Basilan also warrants close monitoring, given both divisions within the governing Hataman clan and internal MILF rifts. Given how prevalent vote buying is in the Philippines, many locals fear that victory will depend on which political bloc has the most cash to dispense. Whether the elections will be free and fair is another question. Given how prevalent vote buying is in the Philippines, many locals fear that victory will depend on which political bloc has the most cash to dispense. Pre-election assessments highlight this risk, warning that it could undermine the election’s legitimacy. Community leaders Crisis Group spoke to also expressed this view. The practice of command votes, under which influential local leaders tell entire communities whom they should vote for, presents another challenge. While mayors and governors are not running in this election, they have an interest in the fortunes of certain candidates, especially if members of their clans are competing. International and domestic entities are working to promote a free and safe poll. Diplomatic representatives of the European Union, Australia, Switzerland, Singapore and Japan will be present in Cotabato City and a handful of nearby locations. Local and international NGOs such as the Independent Election Monitoring Center in Cotabato City, the Legal Network for Truthful Elections, the International Republican Institute, the National Democratic Institute and the Asia Network for Free Elections , are also deploying across the region. They all aim to publish reports of their findings. The national government, moreover, will be dispatching thousands of soldiers and police to the Bangsamoro, with an eye to deterring election-related violence. Some locals , however, view the deployment as overly heavy-handed. What happens after the vote? The major question hovering over these elections is how the MILF and its various factions will fare. The Bangsamoro electorate already had a chance to vote for UBJP-aligned candidates during the 2022 general and local elections , the 2023 village elections , and the 2025 mid-term and local elections. The party’s performance was not impressive; its few successes relied in no small part on local elite backing (either from mayors or village chairs). The MILF’s internal divisions have weakened the UBJP’s chances even further, since they will splinter the vote for the ex-rebels: this time, many local powerbrokers appear to be siding with the Federalist Party or the Grand Coalition. As a result, the most optimistic forecasts say the UBJP will secure only a quarter of parliamentary seats, at best, and about a tenth at worst. While the party could join with smaller parties to muster a majority, the prospect of it being able to rally enough legislators to make up for a poor performance seems unlikely. A more probable scenario is that the Federalist Party or the Grand Coalition achieves a parliamentary majority, possibly with the support of other parties. Both would then back the election of Macacua as chief minister, though the distribution of ministerial positions would hinge on the vote’s outcome. (Parties that garner more votes will presumably lay claim to a greater share of cabinet appointments.) Whether the UBJP will be able to prevent a clan-based coalition from forming a government with Macacua by driving a wedge between the leading political families, or by persuading elected parliamentarians to defect to its ranks when the vote for chief minister takes place, remains an open question. Not surprisingly, some MILF members still hope for reconciliation among the movement’s leaders, though the prospect of that happening seems slim at this juncture. A major loss for the UBJP would be a significant setback for the MILF’s Central Committee. With the MILF leaders ageing, it would fall to mid-level commanders and cadres to build the party into a credible opposition force in the regional parliament over the next five years. A more immediate concern should the UBJP fare poorly is the potential for conflict. Should the MILF rank and file loyal to Murad come to believe that Macacua conspired with Manila to strip the UBJP of its win, aggrieved fighters might turn their frustrations on their former comrades or the national government. The MILF itself could also withdraw from official peace process activities and refuse to disarm. It could even dispatch its troops back to the region’s hills and jungles to express its frustration without resorting to fighting. While successful elections are a crucial step in the peace process, much of the agreement remains unrealised. While successful elections are a crucial step in the peace process, much of the agreement remains unrealised. Rebel and militia demobilisation are stuck in bureaucratic limbo. Manila has pledged to convert former MILF camps into “safe and prosperous communities” by building infrastructure such as roads and starting community-managed economic projects. That effort also lags behind schedule. The same is true of the accord’s transitional justice and amnesty provisions. The government and the peace panel of MILF’s Central Committee, which is aligned with the UBJP and has been in charge of the peace process for the former rebels, have agreed to meet in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur after the vote to discuss implementation of the remaining points of the peace agreement. That might be a sign that Manila is committed to honouring the accord no matter how the elections turn out. Still, there is a growing risk that President Marcos, Jr. will not make the peace process a priority as his term in office starts to wind down. Should the MILF Central Committee’s influence further erode as the splits between ex-rebels widen, Manila may also see little reason to continue treating the movement as an equal partner. For residents of the Bangsamoro, meanwhile, the new regional administration will need to leverage its electoral legitimacy to institute policies that make a material difference in their lives. They are still anxiously waiting for the changes the peace deal promised to start delivering over a decade ago.
